ceutrones.t: Alpine people of the Tarentaise who guarded the Little St Bernard pass and harassed Caesar's army in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.o: The Ceutrones held the upper [[e:isere-river|Isère]] valley, the [[e:tarentaise-valley|Tarentaise]] in [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], below the [[e:little-st-bernard-pass|Little St Bernard]] pass. Caesar records that they and other mountain peoples attacked his legions as they crossed the [[e:alps|Alps]] in 58 BCE.
ceutrones.r: Their power rested on control of the pass, one of the main routes between [[e:gaul|Gaul]] and northern [[e:italy|Italy]], and on herding and trade with the [[s:salassi|Salassi]] of the [[e:aosta-valley|Aosta valley]].
ceutrones.e: They were subdued in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus around 15 BCE and listed on the [[e:tropaeum-alpium|Tropaeum Alpium]]. Their town [[e:aime-savoie|Axima]] (Aime) became Forum [[e:claudia-gens|Claudii]] Ceutronum, capital of the small province of [[e:alpes-graiae|Alpes Graiae]].

colophon.t: Ionian city famed for its cavalry and wealth, home of the poets Mimnermus and Xenophanes and keeper of the oracle of Apollo at Claros.
colophon.o: Colophon lay inland north-west of [[s:ephesus|Ephesus]] and was founded by Ionian settlers c. 1000 BCE. It was one of the twelve cities of the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]] and in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE grew rich and powerful, its exiles seizing [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] from the [[e:aeolians|Aeolians]].
colophon.r: Colophon had a strong landed aristocracy whose cavalry was proverbial. The elegiac poet [[e:mimnermus|Mimnermus]] and the philosopher [[e:xenophanes|Xenophanes]] were Colophonians. The oracle of [[e:apollo|Apollo]] at [[e:claros|Claros]] lay in its territory. [[e:gyges-of-lydia|Gyges]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]] captured its lower town in the 7th century BCE, and it then passed to the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] and the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]].
colophon.e: [[e:lysimachus|Lysimachus]] forced many Colophonians to move to [[s:ephesus|Ephesus]] c. 294 BCE. The city recovered, partly through its port of [[e:notion-ancient-city|Notion]], called New Colophon, and passed to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 133 BCE, while [[e:claros|Claros]] remained a major oracle into Roman times.
colophon.re: Greek religion; oracle of Apollo at Claros

commune-of-volterra.t: An ancient Etruscan hill-city republic whose alum mines provoked a brutal Florentine sack in 1472.
commune-of-volterra.o: Volterra, one of the old Etruscan cities, was long ruled by its [[e:bishop|bishops]]. In the late 12th century its citizens organised a commune, and from 1208 they built the [[e:palazzo-dei-priori-volterra|Palazzo dei Priori]], the oldest surviving town hall in [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]].
commune-of-volterra.r: The commune was governed by consuls, then a podestà and priors, and wrestled with its [[e:bishop|bishops]] for control of the salt pans and mines of its territory. Alabaster carving was an ancient craft. In the 14th century the Belforti family dominated. From 1361 the city was under Florentine protection but kept its own government.
commune-of-volterra.e: A dispute over alum mines led Volterra to rebel in 1472. [[e:federico-da-montefeltro|Federico da Montefeltro]], hired by [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] under [[e:lorenzo-de-medici|Lorenzo de' Medici]], besieged and sacked the city, which was then fully absorbed into the [[s:republic-of-florence|Republic of Florence]].

commune-of-ferrara.t: A Po delta city-republic whose factional wars ended with the Este family as perpetual lords, the start of one of Italy's great dynasties.
commune-of-ferrara.o: [[e:ferrara|Ferrara]] was held by [[e:matilda-of-tuscany|Matilda of Canossa]], who besieged it in 1101 to put down a revolt. In the years that followed, citizens formed a commune under consuls, profiting from Po river traffic and salt. The cathedral was begun in 1135.
commune-of-ferrara.r: [[e:consul|Consuls]] and later a podestà ruled, but power was really contested between noble factions: the Adelardi, the Ghibelline Torelli led by [[e:salinguerra-ii-torelli|Salinguerra II Torelli]], and the Guelph [[e:house-of-este|Este]] marquises. [[e:ferrara|Ferrara's]] position on the Po made it a hub for trade between [[e:venice|Venice]] and the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] plain. [[e:azzo-vii-deste|Azzo VII d'Este]] expelled Salinguerra in 1240 with Venetian and papal help.
commune-of-ferrara.e: After [[e:azzo-vii-deste|Azzo VII]]'s death in 1264, the citizens proclaimed his grandson [[e:obizzo-ii-deste|Obizzo II d'Este]] perpetual lord, and the commune gave way to the [[s:duchy-of-ferrara|Duchy of Ferrara]] under the [[e:house-of-este|Este]].

county-of-zutphen.t: A short-lived county on the IJssel that merged with Guelders in the 12th century and gave its name to one of the duchy's four quarters.
county-of-zutphen.o: The county of Zutphen took shape in the mid-11th century around the trading town on the [[e:ijssel|IJssel]]. Its early counts held lands granted by the German kings and the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]], but details of its first rulers are scarce.
county-of-zutphen.r: Zutphen was a river-trade centre on the route between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the [[e:zuiderzee|Zuiderzee]], and the county included rich farmland in the [[e:achterhoek|Achterhoek]]. Its counts were linked by marriage to the leading families of the region.
county-of-zutphen.e: Around 1138 the heiress Ermgard of Zutphen's marriage to Gerard of Wassenberg, count of [[s:duchy-of-guelders|Guelders]], united Zutphen with the County of Guelders. It became one of the four quarters of the later Duchy of Guelders, and the town of Zutphen joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]].

curacao.t: Island off Venezuela, the former centre of the Dutch Caribbean, which became a separate country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 2010.
curacao.o: When the [[s:netherlands-antilles|Netherlands Antilles]] were dissolved on 10 October 2010, Curaçao became an autonomous country within the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]], after a referendum in 2005 had favoured separate status. [[e:gerrit-schotte|Gerrit Schotte]] became its first prime minister, governing from [[e:willemstad|Willemstad]].
curacao.r: Curaçao has its own parliament, constitution and government, while the kingdom handles defence and foreign affairs, and a shared central bank issues the guilder with [[s:sint-maarten|Sint Maarten]]. The economy rests on tourism, the port, offshore finance and the [[e:isla-refinery|Isla oil refinery]], which was operated by Venezuela's state oil company until 2019 and has stood idle since. [[e:papiamento|Papiamentu]], [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English are official languages. The murder of politician [[e:helmin-wiels|Helmin Wiels]] in 2013 shook public life.
curacao.e: Curaçao remains a country within the kingdom, with [[e:gilmar-pisas|Gilmar Pisas]] as prime minister since 2021. [[e:willemstad|Willemstad's]] colourful colonial harbour is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|World Heritage Site]], and the crisis in neighbouring [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]] has strained its economy and borders.

colony-of-victoria.t: The Australian colony created in 1851 just as gold was found, which made Melbourne one of the richest cities in the world.
colony-of-victoria.o: Settlers from [[s:colony-of-tasmania|Van Diemen's Land]], led by [[e:john-batman|John Batman]] and [[e:john-pascoe-fawkner|John Pascoe Fawkner]], founded [[e:melbourne|Melbourne]] in 1835 on [[e:kulin|Kulin]] land, and the area was governed as the [[e:port-phillip-district|Port Phillip District]] of the [[s:colony-of-new-south-wales|Colony of New South Wales]]. Pressure for separation succeeded in 1851, when Victoria became its own colony under [[e:charles-la-trobe|Charles La Trobe]].
colony-of-victoria.r: Weeks after separation, gold was found at [[e:ballarat|Ballarat]] and [[e:bendigo|Bendigo]], and the population rose from about 77,000 to over 500,000 within a decade. Miners angry at licence fees rebelled at the [[e:eureka-rebellion|Eureka Stockade]] in 1854. Self-government came in 1855, and the secret ballot introduced in 1856 spread worldwide as the 'Australian ballot'. Wool, gold and manufacturing behind [[e:protective-tariff|protective tariffs]] created the wealth of 'Marvellous [[e:melbourne|Melbourne]]' in the 1880s.
colony-of-victoria.e: A land boom collapsed into depression in the early 1890s. Victorian politicians such as [[e:alfred-deakin|Alfred Deakin]] led the movement for federation, and Victoria became a state of the [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Commonwealth of Australia]] in 1901. [[e:melbourne|Melbourne]] served as the temporary national capital until 1927.

county-of-hanau-munzenberg.t: The Main and Wetterau county of the counts of Hanau, whose welcome to Dutch and Walloon refugees in 1597 created the New Town of Hanau.
county-of-hanau-munzenberg.o: The lords of Hanau, raised to counts in 1429, ruled lands around Hanau on the Main and had inherited part of the Münzenberg lordship in the [[e:wetterau|Wetterau]]. In 1458 the county was divided: the elder line kept Hanau-Münzenberg, while a younger line went on to found the [[s:county-of-hanau-lichtenberg|County of Hanau-Lichtenberg]] in [[e:alsace|Alsace]].
county-of-hanau-munzenberg.r: Count [[e:philip-louis-ii-count-of-hanau-munzenberg|Philip Louis II]] adopted [[e:calvinism|Calvinism]] and in 1597 invited Reformed refugees from the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] and [[e:wallonia|Wallonia]] to found the New Town of Hanau, which brought gold-working, [[e:silk|silk]] and other crafts. The county belonged to the [[e:upper-rhenish-circle|Upper Rhenish Circle]]. During the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]] Hanau withstood a long imperial siege, lifted in 1636.
county-of-hanau-munzenberg.e: The Münzenberg line died out in 1642 and its lands passed to the Lichtenberg branch. When the last count, [[e:johann-reinhard-iii-of-hanau|Johann Reinhard III]], died in 1736, Hanau-Münzenberg went to the [[s:landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel|Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel]]. Hanau later became known as the birthplace of the [[e:brothers-grimm|Brothers Grimm]].

catalauni.t: Gallic people of Champagne around Châlons, whose plains gave their name to the battle against Attila in 451.
catalauni.o: The Catalauni are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the [[s:remi|Remi]] in his time. They are known from later Roman sources as a separate community centred on [[e:chalons-en-champagne|Durocatalaunum]] (Châlons-en-Champagne) on the [[e:marne|Marne]].
catalauni.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman rulers. Their chalk plains were rich farmland on the route between [[e:reims|Reims]] and [[e:langres|Langres]].
catalauni.e: [[e:chalons-en-champagne|Durocatalaunum]] became a separate civitas in the late Roman period and a bishopric. The [[e:battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains|Battle of the Catalaunian Plains]] in 451, where [[e:flavius-aetius|Aetius]] and the [[e:visigoths|Visigoths]] halted the [[s:hunnic-empire|Hunnic Empire]] under [[e:attila|Attila]], is named after their land.

county-of-saldana.t: The lordship of the Banu Gómez family on the upper Carrión, powerful nobles of León who sometimes allied with Almanzor.
county-of-saldana.o: In the late 9th and early 10th centuries the Leonese kings granted the lands of [[e:saldana|Saldaña]], [[e:carrion-de-los-condes|Carrión]] and [[e:liebana|Liébana]] on the upper Carrión river to Count Diego Muñoz, founder of the family later called the [[e:banu-gomez|Banu Gómez]] in Arabic sources. The county was part of the resettlement of the [[e:douro|Douro]] plain.
county-of-saldana.r: The counts were among the most powerful nobles of the [[s:kingdom-of-leon|Kingdom of León]], ruling large estates and castles and often rebelling against the crown. Count García Gómez allied with [[e:almanzor|Almanzor]] and took part in his campaigns in the 990s. The county's towns, [[e:saldana|Saldaña]] and [[e:carrion-de-los-condes|Carrión]], lay on the route that became the [[e:camino-de-santiago|Way of St James]].
county-of-saldana.e: After the decline of the [[e:banu-gomez|Banu Gómez]] in the early 11th century, the county passed into the domains of the kings of León and [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]]. [[e:carrion-de-los-condes|Carrión]] later belonged to the Ansúrez family, and its counts appear in the legend of [[e:el-cid|El Cid]].

county-of-lingen.t: A small county on the Ems that passed from the counts of Tecklenburg to the Habsburgs, the house of Orange and finally Prussia.
county-of-lingen.o: Lingen on the Ems belonged to the lands of the [[s:county-of-tecklenburg|County of Tecklenburg]] until a division of the family's territory in the late 15th century made it a separate county under a junior line. Little is known of its earliest years as a separate county.
county-of-lingen.r: Count Konrad of Tecklenburg-Lingen joined the [[e:schmalkaldic-league|Schmalkaldic League]] and introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]; after its defeat [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles V]] confiscated Lingen in 1548 and gave it to [[e:maximilian-of-egmond|Maximilian of Egmond-Buren]], whose heiress married William of [[s:principality-of-orange|Orange]]. Lingen then changed hands between [[e:spain|Spain]] and the house of Orange during the Eighty Years' War, and the [[e:house-of-orange-nassau|Oranges]] founded a Calvinist academy there in 1697.
county-of-lingen.e: When [[e:william-iii-of-england|William III of England]], also prince of [[s:principality-of-orange|Orange]], died in 1702, Lingen passed to his Prussian heir Frederick I and became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]]. It belonged to [[e:hanover|Hanover]] from 1815 to 1866 and is now in [[e:lower-saxony|Lower Saxony]].

cretan-koinon.t: Loose federation of the quarrelsome Cretan city-states, active in the Hellenistic period until the Roman conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE.
cretan-koinon.o: [[e:crete|Crete]] was divided among dozens of independent cities, chief among them [[s:knossos|Knossos]] and [[s:gortyn|Gortyn]], constantly at war. A common body of Cretans (koinon) appears in the 3rd century BCE, and around 216 BCE [[e:philip-v-of-macedon|Philip V of Macedon]] was recognised as its protector (prostates), seeking influence over the island and its [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]].
cretan-koinon.r: The koinon had a council and a common court (koinodikion) to settle disputes between cities, and issued joint decrees and treaties. It never overrode local [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], and wars such as the Lyttian War of the 220s BCE continued. Cretan [[e:archery|archers]] served as [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] across the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], and Cretan ports harboured [[e:piracy|pirates]].
cretan-koinon.e: The league was revived and dissolved several times. [[e:rome|Rome's]] war on piracy brought [[e:marcus-antonius-creticus|Marcus Antonius]]' failed attack in 71 BCE and then [[e:quintus-caecilius-metellus-creticus|Quintus Caecilius Metellus]]' conquest of the island in 69-67 BCE, after which [[e:crete|Crete]] became a Roman province with [[s:gortyn|Gortyn]] as its capital.

county-of-portugal.t: The county of Portucale between the Minho and Douro, founded with the capture of Porto in 868, from which the Kingdom of Portugal was born.
county-of-portugal.o: In 868 [[e:vimara-peres|Vímara Peres]], a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[e:alfonso-iii-of-asturias|Alfonso III of Asturias]], took the town of Portucale ([[e:porto|Porto]]) on the [[e:douro|Douro]] and was made count of the region between the [[e:minho-river|Minho]] and the Douro. His descendants governed it as a frontier county within the [[s:kingdom-of-leon|Kingdom of León]], and Countess [[e:mumadona-dias|Mumadona Dias]] fortified [[e:guimaraes|Guimarães]] in the 10th century.
county-of-portugal.r: The counts ruled a mixed population of Galician-speaking peasants, resettled [[e:mozarabs|Mozarabs]] and frontier warriors. The county was abolished after [[e:garcia-ii-of-galicia|García II of Galicia]] defeated Count [[e:nuno-mendes|Nuno Mendes]] in 1071. In 1096 [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI]] of León recreated it, now including [[e:coimbra|Coimbra]], for [[e:henry-count-of-portugal|Henry of Burgundy]], husband of his daughter [[e:teresa-countess-of-portugal|Teresa]], who ruled after [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] death in 1112.
county-of-portugal.e: [[e:teresa-countess-of-portugal|Teresa]]'s son [[e:afonso-i-of-portugal|Afonso Henriques]] defeated her party at [[e:battle-of-sao-mamede|São Mamede]] in 1128. After his victory at [[e:battle-of-ourique|Ourique]] in 1139 he took the title of king, recognised by León in 1143, and the county became the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]].

county-of-vaduz.t: An Alpine Rhine-valley county that, joined with Schellenberg in 1719, became the Principality of Liechtenstein.
county-of-vaduz.o: The county was created in 1342 when the counts of Werdenberg-Sargans divided their lands and Hartmann III took the territory around Vaduz on the right bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. In 1396 [[e:wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia|King Wenceslaus]] confirmed it as a direct fief of the empire, answerable only to the emperor.
county-of-vaduz.r: Vaduz was a rural county of villages and alpine pastures, ruled from [[e:vaduz-castle|Vaduz Castle]] by its counts and their bailiffs. It passed to the barons of Brandis in 1416, to the counts of Sulz in 1510 and to the [[s:county-of-hohenems|County of Hohenems]] in 1613. Witch trials under the Hohenems counts in the mid and late 17th century were so severe that the emperor intervened and removed the count in 1684.
county-of-vaduz.e: The bankrupt [[s:county-of-hohenems|Hohenems]] counts sold Vaduz in 1712 to [[e:hans-adam-i-prince-of-liechtenstein|Prince Johann Adam Andreas of Liechtenstein]], who had already bought the [[s:lordship-of-schellenberg|Lordship of Schellenberg]]. In 1719 [[e:charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles VI]] united the two as the [[s:principality-of-liechtenstein|Principality of Liechtenstein]], of which Vaduz is the capital today.

county-of-holstein-pinneberg.t: Lower Elbe lordship of the Schauenburg counts, the last branch of Holstein's old rulers, who developed Altona and founded a university at Rinteln.
county-of-holstein-pinneberg.o: The [[s:county-of-schaumburg|Schauenburg]] counts ruled [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] from 1111. When their lands were divided in 1290, one line kept the ancestral County of Schaumburg on the [[e:weser|Weser]] together with the lordship of Pinneberg north of the [[e:elbe|Elbe]] near [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]]. This branch, known as Holstein-Schauenburg or Holstein-Pinneberg, survived after the main Holstein lines merged with [[e:denmark|Denmark]].
county-of-holstein-pinneberg.r: The counts ruled Pinneberg from a distance, with their main residence in Schaumburg at [[e:stadthagen|Stadthagen]] and later [[e:buckeburg|Bückeburg]]. Under them [[e:altona|Altona]] developed beside [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] as a rival trading settlement. Count Ernest, raised to princely rank in 1619, founded a university at [[e:rinteln|Rinteln]] and built the court at Bückeburg. The family adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in the 16th century.
county-of-holstein-pinneberg.e: The line died out with Count Otto V in 1640. Pinneberg and [[e:altona|Altona]] passed to [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Holstein-Gottorp]], while Schaumburg was divided among [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Hesse-Kassel]], Lippe and Brunswick-[[e:luneburg|Lüneburg]].

county-of-hanau-lichtenberg.t: A county straddling the Rhine in northern Alsace and Baden, formed when a branch of the counts of Hanau inherited half of Lichtenberg in 1480.
county-of-hanau-lichtenberg.o: In 1458 the County of [[s:county-of-hanau-munzenberg|Hanau]] was divided, and Philip I the Younger received a share. In 1480 his line inherited half of the lordship of Lichtenberg in northern [[e:alsace|Alsace]] through marriage, forming the County of Hanau-Lichtenberg, with [[e:bouxwiller|Buchsweiler]] (Bouxwiller) as its capital.
county-of-hanau-lichtenberg.r: The counts ruled scattered lands on both banks of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], including the Hanauerland around [[e:kehl|Kehl]]. They introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Lutheran Reformation]] in the 1540s and ran a well-ordered small state. In 1642 they inherited the [[s:county-of-hanau-munzenberg|County of Hanau-Münzenberg]]. From 1680 [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV's]] [[e:reunions|Reunions]] placed the Alsatian lands under French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], though the counts kept their estates and revenues.
county-of-hanau-lichtenberg.e: When the last count, [[e:johann-reinhard-iii-of-hanau|Johann Reinhard III]], died in 1736, Hanau-Lichtenberg passed to the [[s:landgraviate-of-hesse-darmstadt|Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt]]. The French Revolution swept away its Alsatian lordship, and in 1803 the lands east of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] went to [[e:baden|Baden]].

chahamanas-of-ranastambhapura.t: The Chauhan Rajput kingdom of Ranthambore fort, founded after Prithviraj III's defeat and famed for Hammira's defiance of Alauddin Khalji.
chahamanas-of-ranastambhapura.o: After [[e:prithviraj-chauhan|Prithviraj Chauhan]] (Prithviraja III) of the [[s:chahamanas-of-shakambhari|Chahamanas of Shakambhari]] fell to [[e:muhammad-of-ghor|Muhammad of Ghor]] in 1192, his son Govindaraja was installed as a Ghurid [[e:vassal|vassal]] and moved to the fortress of [[e:ranthambore-fort|Ranthambore]] (Ranastambhapura) in eastern [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]]. His descendants ruled there as a separate [[e:chauhan|Chauhan]] line.
chahamanas-of-ranastambhapura.r: The dynasty depended on [[e:ranthambore-fort|Ranthambore]], one of the strongest [[e:hill-fort|hill forts]] of north [[e:india|India]], and alternated between submission to and revolt against the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]; [[e:iltutmish|Iltutmish]] captured the fort in 1226, but the [[e:chauhan|Chauhans]] regained it. [[e:hammira-deva|Hammira]] expanded the kingdom by raids into [[e:malwa|Malwa]] and [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]]. [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] inscriptions and the later epic [[e:hammira-mahakavya|Hammira Mahakavya]] record the dynasty.
chahamanas-of-ranastambhapura.e: [[e:hammira-deva|Hammira]] sheltered Mongol rebels from [[e:alauddin-khalji|Alauddin Khalji's]] army and refused to surrender them. After a long siege [[e:ranthambore-fort|Ranthambore]] fell in 1301 and Hammira was killed. The fall became a celebrated theme of [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] heroic literature; the fort passed to the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]].

county-of-hohnstein.t: County of the southern Harz whose counts, named after Honstein castle, dominated the land around Nordhausen until their line died out in 1593.
county-of-hohnstein.o: The counts took their name from Honstein castle near Neustadt in the southern [[e:harz|Harz]] and appear as a distinct comital house in the later 12th century. They built up lordships around Klettenberg, Lohra and the [[e:goldene-aue|Golden Meadow]], surrounding the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nordhausen|Free Imperial City of Nordhausen]], and for a time also held [[e:sondershausen|Sondershausen]].
county-of-hohnstein.r: The county was a patchwork of castles, villages and forests on the southern edge of the [[e:harz|Harz]], often divided between branches of the family. The counts were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of greater neighbours, including the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[e:halberstadt|Halberstadt]] and the [[e:house-of-wettin|Wettins]], and repeatedly pledged or sold lands to pay debts. Mining and forestry supplemented farming. Like much of [[e:thuringia|Thuringia]], the county adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in the 16th century.
county-of-hohnstein.e: The last count, Ernst VII, died in 1593. His lands were divided among the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick|Duchy of Brunswick]]-[[e:wolfenbuttel|Wolfenbüttel]], the [[e:house-of-schwarzburg|Counts of Schwarzburg]] and the Counts of [[s:county-of-stolberg|Stolberg]], and the Klettenberg and Lohra portions later passed to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] in 1648.

county-of-salona.t: Frankish lordship around Amfissa and Delphi in central Greece that passed from French to Catalan to Byzantine hands before falling to the Ottomans.
county-of-salona.o: [[e:boniface-i-marquis-of-montferrat|Boniface of Montferrat]] granted [[e:amfissa|Salona]], the medieval name of Amfissa, to the French knight Thomas d'Autremencourt in 1205. Its castle, built on the ancient acropolis, controlled the land between [[e:mount-parnassus|Mount Parnassus]] and the [[e:gulf-of-corinth|Gulf of Corinth]], including the old sanctuary of [[s:delphi|Delphi]] and the port of [[e:galaxidi|Galaxidi]].
county-of-salona.r: The lords of [[e:amfissa|Salona]] were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] and neighbours of the [[s:duchy-of-athens|Duchy of Athens]], ruling a Greek peasant population through a small Frankish elite. Thomas III d'Autremencourt was killed in 1311 fighting the [[e:catalan-company|Catalan Company]] at the [[e:battle-of-halmyros|Battle of Halmyros]]. The Catalans took over, and the county later passed to the Fadrique family, a branch of the royal house of [[e:sicily|Sicily]].
county-of-salona.e: In 1394 the widow of [[e:louis-fadrique|Louis Fadrique]], [[e:helena-kantakouzene|Helena Kantakouzene]], lost [[e:amfissa|Salona]] to [[e:bayezid-i|Sultan Bayezid I]]. It was briefly held by the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]] and the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights Hospitaller]] in the early 15th century before the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took it permanently in 1410.

county-of-namur.t: A compact county at the meeting of the Sambre and Meuse, built around a rock fortress that later became one of the most fought-over strongholds in Europe.
county-of-namur.o: Namur emerged in the 10th century from the old district of Lomme, when local counts built their power around the castle on the rock above the [[e:sambre|Sambre]] and [[e:meuse|Meuse]] confluence. Albert I, ruling around 981, is often treated as the first well-documented count, and his family held the county for two centuries.
county-of-namur.r: Namur was a small Walloon county of river trade, forests and ironworks, an imperial fief squeezed between [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Liège]], [[s:county-of-hainaut|Hainaut]], [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]] and [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]]. Count [[e:henry-the-blind|Henry the Blind]] also held Luxembourg in the 12th century. From 1263 the [[e:house-of-dampierre|Dampierre]] counts of [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] ruled it, and Namur's citadel grew into a major fortress.
county-of-namur.e: The bankrupt [[e:john-iii-count-of-namur|John III]] sold Namur to [[e:philip-the-good|Philip the Good]] in 1421, and it joined the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]], then the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]]. [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] took the citadel in 1692 and [[e:william-iii-of-england|William III]] retook it in 1695. [[e:france|France]] annexed the county in 1795; it is now a Belgian province.

county-of-bentheim.t: A Westphalian county on the Dutch border whose sandstone castle and Reformed faith reflected close links to the Netherlands.
county-of-bentheim.o: [[e:bentheim-castle|Bentheim Castle]] appears around 1050 to 1116 on a sandstone ridge on the [[e:vechte|Vechte]] river near the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] border. In the mid 12th century it passed to Otto, a younger son of the counts of Holland, whose descendants ruled it until 1421, when it was inherited by Everwijn of Götterswick, founder of the later house of Bentheim.
county-of-bentheim.r: The county was small and rural, known for Bentheim sandstone, quarried and shipped down the [[e:vechte|Vechte]] to the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], where it was used in buildings such as the Royal Palace of [[e:amsterdam|Amsterdam]]. Count Arnold II introduced the Reformed faith around 1588. The house split into several lines, including Bentheim-Steinfurt and Bentheim-Tecklenburg.
county-of-bentheim.e: Bentheim was pawned to [[e:hanover|Hanover]] from 1753 to 1803. In 1806 the county was mediatised and incorporated into the [[s:grand-duchy-of-berg|Grand Duchy of Berg]], then annexed by [[e:france|France]]. After 1815 it passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]], and today it forms the district of [[e:grafschaft-bentheim|Grafschaft Bentheim]] in [[e:lower-saxony|Lower Saxony]].

clusium.t: Inland Etruscan city whose king Lars Porsenna, in Roman tradition, besieged Rome after the expulsion of the Tarquins.
clusium.o: Clusium, Etruscan Clevsin, modern Chiusi, overlooked the [[e:val-di-chiana|Val di Chiana]], a fertile corridor linking central [[e:etruria|Etruria]] with the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] valley. It developed from Villanovan settlements and flourished from the 7th century BCE, when its distinctive canopic urns, cinerary jars with human-headed lids, show a local elite of growing wealth.
clusium.r: Clusium's power rested on agriculture in the [[e:val-di-chiana|Chiana]] valley and on control of routes towards the interior. Its workshops produced cinerary urns, sculptures in local stone and fine bucchero pottery, while painted tombs such as the Tomb of the Monkey show banquets and games. Roman tradition records its king [[e:lars-porsenna|Lars Porsenna]], who attacked [[e:rome|Rome]] around 508 BCE and possibly took it.
clusium.e: In 391 BCE [[e:gauls|Gauls]] attacked Clusium, an event Roman writers linked to the Gallic sack of [[e:rome|Rome]]. The city came under Roman control after the wars of the early 3rd century, traditionally around the [[e:battle-of-sentinum|battle of Sentinum]] in 295 BCE, and remained a modest Roman town; Etruscan burials continued there into the 1st century BCE.

county-of-artois.t: A northern French county of cloth towns and tapestries, created as a royal appanage and later held by Burgundy and Spain before returning to France.
county-of-artois.o: Artois came to the French crown in 1191 through [[e:isabella-of-hainaut|Isabella of Hainaut's]] dowry. In 1237 [[e:louis-ix-of-france|Louis IX]] created it as a county for his brother Robert I, who was killed at [[e:battle-of-al-mansurah|Mansourah]] in 1250 on [[e:crusade|crusade]]. Robert's descendants ruled it from [[e:arras|Arras]].
county-of-artois.r: [[e:arras|Arras]] was a major cloth and banking town, and its tapestries became so famous that 'arras' meant a wall hanging in English and Italian. Count [[e:robert-ii-count-of-artois|Robert II]] was killed at [[e:kortrijk|Courtrai]] in 1302, and his daughter [[e:mahaut-countess-of-artois|Mahaut]] defended her inheritance against her nephew [[e:robert-iii-of-artois|Robert III]]. In 1384 Artois passed with [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] to [[e:philip-the-bold|Philip the Bold]], joining the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]].
county-of-artois.e: After 1477 Artois stayed with the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] in the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]] and [[s:spanish-netherlands|Spanish Netherlands]]. [[e:louis-xiii-of-france|Louis XIII]] took [[e:arras|Arras]] in 1640, and the [[e:treaty-of-the-pyrenees|Treaty of the Pyrenees]] of 1659 gave most of the county to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

clanricarde.t: The Gaelicised Burke lordship of south Galway, ruled by the Mac William Uachtar, which became an earldom under Henry VIII in 1543.
clanricarde.o: When [[e:william-donn-de-burgh-3rd-earl-of-ulster|William Donn de Burgh]], Earl of [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]], was murdered in 1333, his [[s:kingdom-of-connacht|Connacht]] lands were seized by his kinsmen. The southern branch, led by [[e:ulick-de-burgh|Ulick de Burgh]], adopted the Gaelic title Mac William Uachtar, the Upper Mac William, and ruled south [[e:galway|Galway]] from [[e:loughrea|Loughrea]].
clanricarde.r: The Clanricarde [[e:house-of-burgh|Burkes]] adopted Irish law, language and customs, intermarrying with Gaelic families while competing with the [[e:obrien-dynasty|O'Briens]] and with [[e:galway|Galway]] town. Their battles included [[e:battle-of-knockdoe|Knockdoe]] in 1504, where [[e:ulick-fionn-burke|Ulick Fionn Burke]] was defeated by the [[e:gerald-fitzgerald-8th-earl-of-kildare|Earl of Kildare]]. Tower houses dotted their lands.
clanricarde.e: In 1543 [[e:ulick-na-gceann-burke-1st-earl-of-clanricarde|Ulick na gCeann Burke]] submitted to [[e:henry-viii-of-england|Henry VIII]] and became [[e:earl-of-clanricarde|Earl of Clanricarde]] in the [[s:kingdom-of-ireland|Kingdom of Ireland]]. Later earls were loyal to the crown, and [[e:ulick-burke-1st-marquess-of-clanricarde|Ulick Burke]] was made Marquess of Clanricarde in 1646.

commune-of-padua.t: A Venetian-plain city-republic that founded Italy's second university in 1222 and saw Giotto paint the Scrovegni Chapel.
commune-of-padua.o: [[e:padua|Padua]], a large Roman town that had recovered slowly from the early [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]], had consuls by 1138. The commune took power from its [[e:bishop|bishop]] and expanded across the plain between the [[e:brenta|Brenta]] and the [[e:adige|Adige]].
commune-of-padua.r: Governed by consuls and later a podestà, [[e:padua|Padua]] joined the [[s:lombard-league|Lombard League]]. In 1222 masters and students from [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] founded its university. From 1237 to 1256 the city suffered under [[e:ezzelino-iii-da-romano|Ezzelino III da Romano]]. Afterwards the commune flourished: the basilica of Saint Anthony was built, [[e:giotto|Giotto]] painted the [[e:scrovegni-chapel|Scrovegni Chapel]] around 1305, and the scholar [[e:albertino-mussato|Albertino Mussato]] revived classical [[e:latin|Latin]] drama. Padua ruled [[s:commune-of-vicenza|Vicenza]] for a time.
commune-of-padua.e: Pressure from [[e:cangrande-i-della-scala|Cangrande della Scala]] of [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]] led the citizens in 1318 to make [[e:jacopo-i-da-carrara|Jacopo I da Carrara]] their lord, beginning the [[s:lordship-of-padua|Lordship of Padua]].

county-of-cerdanya.t: A Pyrenean county of the Catalan heartland whose counts founded Sant Martí del Canigó before it passed to Barcelona in 1117.
county-of-cerdanya.o: The high valley of [[e:cerdanya|Cerdanya]] came under Frankish rule around 798 and was organised as a county of the [[s:marca-hispanica|Marca Hispanica]], often held with neighbouring Urgell. [[e:sunifred-of-urgell|Sunifred]], father of [[e:wilfred-the-hairy|Wilfred the Hairy]], held it in the 830s and 840s, and Wilfred himself became count in 870.
county-of-cerdanya.r: From 897 [[e:cerdanya|Cerdanya]] had its own line of counts descended from [[e:wilfred-the-hairy|Wilfred]], controlling the valley, [[e:conflent|Conflent]], [[e:berga|Berga]] and [[e:monastery-of-santa-maria-de-ripoll|Ripoll]]. The counts were great patrons of the church: [[e:wifred-ii-of-cerdanya|Wifred II]] founded the monastery of [[e:sant-marti-del-canigo|Sant Martí del Canigó]] around 1009, and his brother [[e:oliba|Oliba]] became abbot of Ripoll and [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Vic. The county lived from mountain herding and Pyrenean trade routes.
county-of-cerdanya.e: When Count [[e:bernat-guillem-of-cerdanya|Bernat Guillem]] died without heirs in 1117, [[e:cerdanya|Cerdanya]] passed to [[e:ramon-berenguer-iii-of-barcelona|Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona]]. It became part of the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]], and in 1659 the [[e:treaty-of-the-pyrenees|Treaty of the Pyrenees]] split the valley between [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[e:france|France]].

corduene.t: A mountain kingdom south of Lake Van that lay on the fault line between Rome and Iran, changing hands in their treaties for four centuries.
corduene.o: Corduene (Gordyene) occupied the rugged mountains of the upper [[e:tigris|Tigris]], around modern [[e:cizre|Cizre]] and the [[s:emirate-of-bohtan|Botan]] region. [[e:xenophon|Xenophon]] met its warlike inhabitants, the [[e:carduchi|Carduchi]], in 401 BCE. A kingdom appears in the 1st century BCE, when [[e:tigranes-the-great|Tigranes the Great]] of [[s:armenia|Armenia]] annexed it.
corduene.r: Its rulers were local kings or [[e:satrapy|satraps]] who depended on stronger neighbours, [[s:armenia|Armenia]], the [[s:parthian-empire|Parthian Empire]] and [[e:rome|Rome]]. [[e:plutarch|Plutarch]] records that King [[e:zarbienus|Zarbienus]] negotiated secretly with Rome and was put to death by [[e:tigranes-the-great|Tigranes]], after which [[e:lucius-licinius-lucullus|Lucullus]] honoured his memory. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] spread there in late antiquity. The name has often been linked with that of the [[e:kurds|Kurds]], but the connection is uncertain.
corduene.e: By the Peace of [[e:nisibis|Nisibis]] in 298 Corduene passed to the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]]; in 363 Jovian returned it to the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]], which absorbed it as a province, with its autonomy fading by the late 4th century.

commonwealth-of-the-philippines.t: Self-governing Philippine state of 1935 to 1946 that prepared the country for independence and survived Japanese occupation in exile.
commonwealth-of-the-philippines.o: The [[e:tydings-mcduffie-act|Tydings-McDuffie Act]] of 1934 provided for a ten-year transition to independence. Filipinos drafted and ratified a constitution in 1935, and on 15 November 1935 [[e:manuel-l-quezon|Manuel L. Quezon]] was inaugurated as president, with [[e:sergio-osmena|Sergio Osmena]] as vice-president, replacing the [[s:insular-government-of-the-philippine-islands|Insular Government of the Philippine Islands]].
commonwealth-of-the-philippines.r: The Commonwealth had its own president, legislature and courts, while the [[s:united-states|United States]] kept control of foreign affairs and defence through a high commissioner. [[e:manuel-l-quezon|Quezon]] promoted social justice programmes, women gained the vote in 1937, and [[e:tagalog-language|Tagalog]] was chosen as the basis of a national language. [[e:douglas-macarthur|Douglas MacArthur]] built up a Philippine army.
commonwealth-of-the-philippines.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] invaded in December 1941, and after the fall of [[e:battle-of-bataan|Bataan]] and [[e:battle-of-corregidor-1942|Corregidor]] the government went into exile in [[e:washington-dc|Washington]]. [[e:manuel-l-quezon|Quezon]] died in 1944, and [[e:sergio-osmena|Osmena]] returned with American forces at [[e:battle-of-leyte|Leyte]]. The Commonwealth ended when the [[s:philippines|Philippines]] became independent on 4 July 1946.

cretan-state.t: Autonomous Crete under great-power protection from 1898, a stepping stone to union with Greece and the launch pad of Eleftherios Venizelos.
cretan-state.o: [[e:crete|Crete]] rose repeatedly against Ottoman rule in the 19th century. After the revolt of 1897 and the [[e:greco-turkish-war-1897|Greco-Turkish War]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], [[e:france|France]], [[e:russia|Russia]] and [[e:italy|Italy]] occupied the island and forced the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] to accept its autonomy under nominal suzerainty. [[e:prince-george-of-greece-and-denmark|Prince George of Greece]] became High Commissioner in December 1898, with [[s:kydonia|Chania]] as capital.
cretan-state.r: The Cretan State had its own constitution, assembly, gendarmerie, currency and stamps, though foreign troops remained. Prince George's autocratic style clashed with [[e:eleftherios-venizelos|Eleftherios Venizelos]], who led the [[e:theriso-revolt|Therisos revolt]] in 1905. [[e:alexandros-zaimis|Alexandros Zaimis]] replaced the prince in 1906. Most of the population was Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]], with a significant Muslim minority.
cretan-state.e: In 1908 the Cretan assembly declared union with [[e:greece|Greece]]. After the [[e:balkan-wars|Balkan Wars]], the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] renounced [[e:crete|Crete]], and it was formally united with the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]] in December 1913. [[e:eleftherios-venizelos|Venizelos]] had by then become prime minister of Greece.

county-of-tripoli.t: The last Crusader state to be founded, a Lebanese coastal county that held Krak des Chevaliers and lasted until 1289.
county-of-tripoli.o: [[e:raymond-iv-of-toulouse|Raymond of Saint-Gilles]], count of [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]], besieged Tripoli from 1102, building the castle of [[e:mount-pilgrim|Mount Pilgrim]] outside the city, but died in 1105. His son [[e:bertrand-of-toulouse|Bertrand]] took the city from the [[s:banu-ammar-of-tripoli|Banu Ammar]] in July 1109, and the county was formed as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-jerusalem|Kingdom of Jerusalem]].
county-of-tripoli.r: The county ran along the coast from [[e:byblos|Jubail]] to [[e:tartus|Tortosa]] and inland to the [[e:orontes-river|Orontes]]. Its counts, from the house of [[s:county-of-toulouse|Toulouse]], gave the Hospitallers [[e:krak-des-chevaliers|Krak des Chevaliers]] in 1142, and the military orders came to hold much of the frontier. [[e:raymond-iii-of-tripoli|Raymond III]] was regent of [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] in the 1170s and 1180s. [[e:tripoli|Tripoli's]] [[e:silk|silk]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and paper industries continued under Frankish rule. From the early 13th century the county was united with the [[s:principality-of-antioch|Principality of Antioch]].
county-of-tripoli.e: [[e:krak-des-chevaliers|Krak des Chevaliers]] fell to [[e:baybars|Baybars]] in 1271. The [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] sultan [[e:qalawun|Qalawun]] stormed [[e:tripoli|Tripoli]] in April 1289, and a new city was built inland.

canton-of-seville.t: A short-lived revolutionary canton proclaimed in Seville during the federalist Cantonal Rebellion of 1873.
canton-of-seville.o: In July 1873, impatient with the slow progress of federalism under the [[s:spanish-first-republic|Spanish First Republic]], radical federalists across southern and eastern [[e:spain|Spain]] declared their cities sovereign cantons. [[e:seville|Seville's]] federalists proclaimed their canton on 19 July 1873.
canton-of-seville.r: The cantonal junta took control of the city, raised volunteer militias and announced radical measures, including the seizure of church property and workers' reforms, intending to form part of a future federal [[e:spain|Spain]] built from the bottom up.
canton-of-seville.e: Government troops under General [[e:manuel-pavia-y-rodriguez-de-alburquerque|Manuel Pavía]] attacked the city and, after street fighting, crushed the canton at the end of July 1873. Pavía went on to subdue the [[s:canton-of-cadiz|Canton of Cádiz]].

county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.t: Small Westphalian county in the Rothaar hills, known as a refuge for radical Pietists and as home of the Berleburg Bible.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.o: The [[s:county-of-sayn|County of Sayn]]-[[e:ludwig-wittgenstein|Wittgenstein]] was divided in 1605 among the sons of Count Ludwig I. Georg received [[e:bad-berleburg|Berleburg]] in the northern Wittgenstein land, founding a line that would persist alongside Sayn-Wittgenstein-Hohenstein.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.r: The county was poor, forested upland with some iron working, governed from [[e:berleburg-castle|Berleburg Castle]]. Under Count Casimir in the early 18th century it became a haven for religious dissenters and radical [[e:pietism|Pietists]], and the eight-volume [[e:berleburg-bible|Berleburg Bible]], a mystical commentary, was published there from 1726. The counts were raised to princely rank in 1792.
county-of-sayn-wittgenstein-berleburg.e: The territory was mediatised in 1806 and placed under the [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Grand Duchy of Hesse]], then passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]] in 1816 as part of the [[e:province-of-westphalia|Province of Westphalia]]. The princes of Sayn-Wittgenstein-[[e:bad-berleburg|Berleburg]] still live at [[e:berleburg-castle|Berleburg Castle]].
