county-of-erbach.t: An Odenwald county of the Schenks of Erbach, whose castle holds a famous collection of antiquities and whose town became known for ivory carving.
county-of-erbach.o: The lords of Erbach served as hereditary [[e:cupbearer|cupbearers]] (Schenken) of the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]] and built up lands in the [[e:odenwald|Odenwald]] from the 12th century. In 1532 [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Charles V]] raised them to imperial counts, and their territory became the County of Erbach.
county-of-erbach.r: The counts adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in the 1540s and ruled a wooded upland territory of small towns and villages, often divided among branches such as Erbach-Fürstenau, Erbach-Erbach and Erbach-Schönberg. At the end of the 18th century Count Franz I gathered antiquities, armour and antlers at Erbach castle and in 1783 founded the [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]]-carving craft that became the town's speciality.
county-of-erbach.e: In 1806 the county was mediatised and placed under the [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Grand Duchy of Hesse]]. The counts kept their castles, and Erbach is still known for its carving museum and craft.

cofitachequi.t: A Mississippian chiefdom in South Carolina, famed for the woman ruler who received Hernando de Soto with gifts of freshwater pearls in 1540.
cofitachequi.o: Cofitachequi arose among Mississippian farming towns on the [[e:wateree-river|Wateree River]] in central [[e:south-carolina|South Carolina]], with its main centre probably at the Mulberry mound site near modern [[e:camden-south-carolina|Camden]]. By the 14th century it had become the leading power of the region, and its paramount chief claimed authority over towns across much of the [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] piedmont and coastal plain.
cofitachequi.r: In 1540 [[e:hernando-de-soto|Hernando de Soto's]] army was met by a woman ruler, known to the Spanish as the Lady of Cofitachequi, who presented strings of pearls; the Spanish looted pearls from a temple-burial house and took her hostage, though she escaped. Spanish accounts describe towns with mounds, granaries of [[e:maize|maize]] and stored deerskins and textiles. [[e:juan-pardo-explorer|Juan Pardo]] passed through in 1566 to 1568.
cofitachequi.e: Epidemics and the Spanish and later English [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] weakened the chiefdom. When the English trader [[e:henry-woodward-colonist|Henry Woodward]] visited in 1670 it was still recognised but much smaller, and it vanished soon after, its people probably merging with the [[e:catawba-people|Catawba]] and other piedmont groups.

county-of-evreux.t: A Norman county that became the appanage of a royal branch whose members, as kings of Navarre, schemed against the Valois.
county-of-evreux.o: Around 989 Duke [[e:richard-i-of-england|Richard I]] of [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Normandy]] created the county of [[e:evreux|Évreux]] for his son Robert, archbishop of [[e:rouen|Rouen]]. Robert's descendants held it as major Norman barons, and it later passed to the [[s:county-of-montfort|Montfort]] family, frequently caught up in the wars between Normandy and [[e:france|France]].
county-of-evreux.r: [[e:evreux|Évreux]] was a rich farming district on the road from [[e:paris|Paris]] to [[e:rouen|Rouen]], with a cathedral city as its centre. [[e:philip-ii-of-france|Philip II]] obtained it from [[e:john-king-of-england|John of England]] by the [[e:treaty-of-le-goulet|Treaty of Le Goulet]] in 1200. In 1307 [[e:philip-iv-of-france|Philip IV]] gave it as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] to his half-brother Louis, whose son married [[e:joan-ii-of-navarre|Joan II of Navarre]], founding the Évreux kings of [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]].
county-of-evreux.e: [[e:charles-ii-of-navarre|Charles the Bad]] of [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]] used [[e:evreux|Évreux]] as a base for his intrigues against [[e:john-ii-of-france|John II]] and [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]], who seized most of his Norman lands. In 1404 his son [[e:charles-iii-of-navarre|Charles III of Navarre]] exchanged Évreux with [[e:charles-vi-of-france|Charles VI]] for the duchy of [[e:duchy-of-nemours|Nemours]], and it returned to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

captaincy-of-sao-paulo.t: The royal captaincy created around São Paulo after the gold rush, from which the captaincies of Brazil's interior were carved and where independence was declared.
captaincy-of-sao-paulo.o: After [[e:war-of-the-emboabas|the War of the Emboabas]] between Paulista pioneers and newcomers in the gold fields, the crown bought out the old [[s:captaincy-of-sao-vicente|Captaincy of São Vicente]] and created the Captaincy of [[e:sao-paulo|São Paulo]] and [[e:meena|Minas]] de Ouro in 1709, with São Paulo as its capital. It covered much of southern and central [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]].
captaincy-of-sao-paulo.r: The vast captaincy was soon divided: [[s:captaincy-of-minas-gerais|Minas Gerais]] was separated in 1720, then [[e:goias-velho|Goiás]] in 1744 and [[s:captaincy-of-mato-grosso|Mato Grosso]] in 1748. In 1748 [[e:sao-paulo|São Paulo]] itself lost its governor and was placed under [[e:rio-de-janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]]. It was restored in 1765 under the [[e:luis-antonio-de-sousa-botelho-mourao|Morgado de Mateus]], who promoted [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] cultivation. Paulista society was rooted in the bandeirante tradition, with mule trains linking the south to the mines.
captaincy-of-sao-paulo.e: In 1821 the captaincy became a province. On 7 September 1822, by the [[e:ipiranga-river|Ipiranga]] stream in [[e:sao-paulo|São Paulo]], Prince Pedro proclaimed [[e:brazil|Brazil's]] independence, and the province joined the [[e:brazilian-empire|Empire of Brazil]], later becoming its economic powerhouse through [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]].

cr.a: Tonyjeff, based on ancient national symbol.

chandra-dynasty.t: A Buddhist dynasty of eastern Bengal that ruled Harikela and Vanga from Vikramapura in the 10th and 11th centuries.
chandra-dynasty.o: The Chandras rose in the early 10th century in [[e:harikela|Harikela]], the region around [[e:chittagong|Chittagong]] and [[e:comilla|Comilla]] in modern [[s:bangladesh|Bangladesh]]. [[e:trailokyachandra|Trailokyachandra]] extended their rule over [[e:vanga|Vanga]], and his son [[e:shrichandra|Shrichandra]] moved the capital to [[e:vikramapura|Vikramapura]] near [[e:dhaka|Dhaka]], ruling a kingdom independent of the [[s:pala-empire|Pala Empire]].
chandra-dynasty.r: The Chandras were Buddhists who endowed monasteries, and the excavated monasteries of [[e:mainamati|Mainamati]] near [[e:comilla|Comilla]] flourished in their time. Their [[e:copper|copper]]-plate grants, such as the Rampal plate of [[e:shrichandra|Shrichandra]], record gifts to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] as well. The kingdom had access to the trade of the [[e:bay-of-bengal|Bay of Bengal]] through [[e:chittagong|Chittagong]] and [[e:samatata|Samatata]].
chandra-dynasty.e: Around 1021 to 1024 the army of [[e:rajendra-chola-i|Rajendra I]] of the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] defeated [[e:govindachandra-of-the-chandra-dynasty|Govindachandra]] during its march to the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]]. The dynasty ended by the mid-11th century and was succeeded in eastern [[e:bengal|Bengal]] by the [[s:varman-dynasty-of-bengal|Varman dynasty of Bengal]].

county-of-pyrmont.t: Small Weser Uplands county built around Pyrmont castle and its mineral springs, which grew into one of Germany's most fashionable spas.
county-of-pyrmont.o: Archbishop [[e:philip-i-archbishop-of-cologne|Philip of Heinsberg]] of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] had Pyrmont castle built around 1184 to secure his new Westphalian ducal power, and a family of counts took their name from it as [[e:cologne|Cologne's]] [[e:vassal|vassals]]. The territory lay around the springs in the valley of the Emmer, known since antiquity.
county-of-pyrmont.r: The county was small and agrarian. Its main asset was the mineral water: in 1556 a sudden fame of the healing springs drew thousands of pilgrims, and later the spa attracted nobility and royalty. After the original line died out in 1494 the county passed to the counts of Spiegelberg and then to the counts of Gleichen, and became Lutheran.
county-of-pyrmont.e: With the extinction of the Gleichen line in 1625, Pyrmont was inherited by the counts of Waldeck and ruled with the [[s:principality-of-waldeck|Principality of Waldeck]] as Waldeck-Pyrmont. It joined [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia's]] [[e:province-of-hanover|Province of Hanover]] in 1922 and is now [[e:bad-pyrmont|Bad Pyrmont]] in [[e:lower-saxony|Lower Saxony]].

colonia-del-sacramento.t: A Portuguese outpost on the River Plate opposite Buenos Aires that changed hands repeatedly as Spain and Portugal fought for the estuary.
colonia-del-sacramento.o: In 1680 the Portuguese governor of [[e:rio-de-janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] sent [[e:manuel-lobo|Manuel Lobo]] to found Colônia do Santíssimo Sacramento on the northern bank of the [[e:rio-de-la-plata|River Plate]], directly across from [[e:buenos-aires|Buenos Aires]]. [[e:spain|Spain]] captured it within months, but a treaty of 1681 returned it to Portugal.
colonia-del-sacramento.r: Colonia was a fortified town and a base for smuggling: Portuguese and British goods and enslaved Africans flowed into the Spanish territories in exchange for [[e:silver|silver]] from [[e:potosi|Potosí]] and hides. Its presence provoked [[e:spain|Spain]] to found [[e:montevideo|Montevideo]] in 1724. Spanish forces besieged it in 1704, 1735 and 1762. By the [[e:treaty-of-madrid-1750|Treaty of Madrid]] of 1750 Portugal agreed to exchange it for the Seven Missions, but the deal collapsed.
colonia-del-sacramento.e: [[e:pedro-de-cevallos|Pedro de Cevallos]] captured Colonia for the last time in 1777, and the [[e:first-treaty-of-san-ildefonso|Treaty of San Ildefonso]] that year confirmed Spanish possession. It became part of [[s:oriental-republic-of-uruguay|Uruguay]]. Its historic quarter, with Portuguese and Spanish streets, became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1995.

county-of-luxembourg.t: The castle-county on the Alzette that gave the Holy Roman Empire three emperors and grew into the duchy behind today's Grand Duchy.
county-of-luxembourg.o: In 963 Count [[e:siegfried-count-of-luxembourg|Siegfried]] acquired the rock of Lucilinburhuc from the abbey of St Maximin at [[e:trier|Trier]] and built a castle there. His descendants, and from 1136 the counts of [[s:county-of-namur|Namur]] and later [[s:duchy-of-limburg|Limburg]] lines, expanded the county through the [[e:ardennes|Ardennes]] and [[e:moselle|Moselle]] valley.
county-of-luxembourg.r: [[s:grand-duchy-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] was a bilingual land of German and French speakers. Count [[e:henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor|Henry VII]] became emperor in 1308, and his son [[e:john-of-bohemia|John the Blind]], king of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], died at [[e:battle-of-crecy|Crécy]] in 1346. [[e:charles-iv|Emperor Charles IV]] raised the county to a duchy in 1354. The fortress city became one of [[e:europe|Europe's]] strongest, later rebuilt by Vauban.
county-of-luxembourg.e: [[e:elisabeth-of-gorlitz|Elisabeth of Görlitz]] ceded the duchy to [[e:philip-the-good|Philip the Good]] of the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]] in 1443. It then passed with the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]] to the [[s:spanish-netherlands|Spanish Netherlands]] and [[s:austrian-netherlands|Austrian Netherlands]], was briefly French in 1684–1697, and was annexed by [[e:france|France]] in 1795. It was revived as the [[s:grand-duchy-of-luxembourg|Grand Duchy of Luxembourg]] in 1815.

colony-of-liberia.t: The settlement founded by the American Colonization Society for free Black Americans at Cape Mesurado, which became the independent Republic of Liberia in 1847.
colony-of-liberia.o: The [[e:american-colonization-society|American Colonization Society]], founded in 1816, aimed to settle free Black Americans in [[e:africa|Africa]]. In December 1821 its agents Eli Ayres and [[e:robert-f-stockton|Robert Stockton]] pressed local Dei rulers, including King Peter, to cede [[e:cape-mesurado|Cape Mesurado]], and settlers landed in 1822. The settlement was named [[e:monrovia|Monrovia]] after President [[e:james-monroe|James Monroe]], and the colony was named [[s:liberia|Liberia]] in 1824.
colony-of-liberia.r: The society appointed white agents, notably [[e:jehudi-ashmun|Jehudi Ashmun]], who organised defence and trade, while settlers gradually gained a role in government. Other societies founded separate colonies: [[s:bassa-cove|Bassa Cove]] joined the Commonwealth of [[s:liberia|Liberia]] in 1839, and [[s:mississippi-in-africa|Mississippi-in-Africa]] followed in 1842. Settlers, known as [[e:americo-liberians|Americo-Liberians]], dominated politics and trade, often in conflict with indigenous peoples. [[e:joseph-jenkins-roberts|Joseph Jenkins Roberts]] became the first Black governor in 1841.
colony-of-liberia.e: Disputes with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] over customs duties showed that a private society's colony lacked standing as a state. On 26 July 1847 the colony declared independence as [[s:liberia|Liberia]], with [[e:joseph-jenkins-roberts|Roberts]] as its first president.

commune-of-cremona.t: A rich Po valley city-republic, usually loyal to the emperors and Milan's great rival, crowned by the Torrazzo bell tower.
commune-of-cremona.o: Cremona's citizens won rights from their [[e:bishop|bishop]] in the late 11th century, and consuls are recorded from 1098. Commanding a crossing of the Po, the city became a major river port and soon clashed with [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] and its ally [[e:crema|Crema]].
commune-of-cremona.r: Cremona was governed by consuls and later a podestà, with a strong [[e:guild|guild]] of merchants and cloth makers. It generally sided with the emperors: it helped [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] destroy [[e:crema|Crema]] in 1160 and was a key base for Frederick II. The [[e:torrazzo-of-cremona|Torrazzo]], one of the tallest medieval bell towers in [[e:italy|Italy]], and the cathedral date from this period. In the 13th century Ghibelline strongmen such as [[e:buoso-da-dovara|Buoso da Dovara]] and [[e:uberto-pallavicino|Uberto Pallavicino]] held power.
commune-of-cremona.e: Faction struggles between the Cavalcabò and their rivals weakened the commune, and in 1334 it submitted to [[e:azzone-visconti|Azzone Visconti]], becoming part of the [[s:lordship-of-milan|Lordship of Milan]].

county-of-bigorre.t: Small Pyrenean county around Tarbes and Lourdes, remembered for one of the oldest charters of customs in France.
county-of-bigorre.o: Bigorre, the land of the ancient [[s:bigerriones|Bigerriones]], became a county under the [[e:carolingian-empire|Carolingians]] in the 9th century, at the edge of the [[s:duchy-of-gascony|Duchy of Gascony]]. Its first counts are poorly documented, and their line was linked with the rulers of [[e:gascony|Gascony]] and [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]].
county-of-bigorre.r: The county controlled the upper [[e:adour|Adour]] valley and passes into [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], with [[e:tarbes|Tarbes]] as its seat and the castle of [[e:lourdes|Lourdes]] as its stronghold. The [[e:fors-de-bigorre|Fors de Bigorre]], granted around 1097, set out the rights of the inhabitants and limits on comital power. In the 13th century Countess [[e:petronilla-countess-of-bigorre|Petronilla]] married five times, leaving a bitter succession dispute.
county-of-bigorre.e: Bigorre passed through several hands, including English rule after 1360, before falling to the House of Foix-Béarn in the 15th century and then to the [[e:house-of-albret|Albret]] kings of [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]]. When [[e:henry-iv-of-france|Henry of Navarre]] became Henry IV of [[e:france|France]], it was united with the crown in 1607.

county-of-monzon.t: A Leonese frontier county on the Tierra de Campos, created for the Ansúrez family as a counterweight to Castile.
county-of-monzon.o: Around 943 [[e:ramiro-ii-of-leon|Ramiro II of León]] created the County of [[e:monzon-de-campos|Monzón]], around [[e:monzon|Monzón]] de Campos near [[e:palencia|Palencia]], for [[e:assur-fernandez|Assur Fernández]], a rival of [[e:fernan-gonzalez-of-castile|Fernán González of Castile]]. It was part of the king's effort to check the growing independence of [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
county-of-monzon.r: The Ansúrez counts governed a fertile plain of the [[e:tierra-de-campos|Tierra de Campos]], newly resettled by farmers, from the castle of [[e:monzon-de-campos|Monzón]]. They were among the leading nobles of the [[s:kingdom-of-leon|Kingdom of León]], involved in its civil wars and frontier fighting against the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]].
county-of-monzon.e: After Fernando Ansúrez, the county passed by marriage and conflict into the hands of other families and was absorbed into the domains of the kings of León and [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] by the early 11th century. The Ansúrez family later produced [[e:pedro-ansurez|Pedro Ansúrez]], the lord who developed [[e:valladolid|Valladolid]].

coriondi.t: People of south-east Ireland known only from Ptolemy's Geography, whose name may be related to later Irish population names.
coriondi.o: The Coriondi appear in [[e:geography-ptolemy|Ptolemy's Geography]] of about 150, placed in the interior of south-eastern Ireland, roughly in modern Counties [[e:county-kilkenny|Kilkenny]], [[e:county-carlow|Carlow]] or [[e:county-wexford|Wexford]], near the [[s:brigantes-ireland|Brigantes (Ireland)]] and the [[s:usdiae|Usdiae]]. As with his other Irish peoples, his information came from earlier sailors' and traders' reports.
coriondi.r: Nothing is known of their government or way of life. Some scholars have compared their name with the Coraind, a group mentioned in early Irish texts, or with British names built on the element coria, meaning a war band or host, but no identification is certain.
coriondi.e: The Coriondi disappear from the record after Ptolemy. Their region later fell within the [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Kingdom of Leinster]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-osraige|Kingdom of Osraige]].

county-of-lowenstein-wertheim.t: A Franconian county formed when a morganatic branch of the Wittelsbachs inherited Wertheim on the Main in 1574.
county-of-lowenstein-wertheim.o: The counts of [[e:house-of-lowenstein-wertheim|Löwenstein]] descended from Elector [[e:frederick-i-elector-palatine|Frederick I of the Palatinate]] and his morganatic wife Clara Tott. Count Ludwig III of Löwenstein married [[e:anna-ii-abbess-of-quedlinburg|Anna of Stolberg]], heiress to the county of [[s:county-of-wertheim|Wertheim]], and in 1574 the couple took possession of Wertheim, creating Löwenstein-Wertheim.
county-of-lowenstein-wertheim.r: The counts ruled lands on the Main around [[s:county-of-wertheim|Wertheim]] and elsewhere in [[e:franconia|Franconia]] from the castle above the town. In 1611 the family split into a Protestant line, later called [[e:house-of-lowenstein-wertheim|Löwenstein]]-Wertheim-Virneburg and then Freudenberg, and a Catholic line, Löwenstein-Wertheim-Rochefort, raised to princes in 1711, which shared Wertheim. The territory belonged to the [[e:franconian-circle|Franconian Circle]].
county-of-lowenstein-wertheim.e: In 1806 both lines were mediatised and their lands divided mainly between [[e:baden|Baden]] and [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]]. The princely families survive, and the ruined castle above [[s:county-of-wertheim|Wertheim]] and the palace at Kleinheubach remain their landmarks.

colony-of-trinidad.t: British colony on Trinidad, captured from Spain in 1797, ruled directly by the crown and transformed by Indian indentured migration after slavery ended.
colony-of-trinidad.o: [[s:spanish-trinidad|Spanish Trinidad]] had been thinly settled until the [[e:cedula-of-population|Cédula de Población]] of 1783 drew French Catholic planters and their enslaved workers. In February 1797 a British force under [[e:ralph-abercromby|Sir Ralph Abercromby]] captured the island almost without resistance, and the [[e:treaty-of-amiens|Treaty of Amiens]] in 1802 confirmed the cession.
colony-of-trinidad.r: [[e:trinidad|Trinidad]] became an experimental crown colony with no elected assembly, run by governors such as the harsh [[e:thomas-picton|Thomas Picton]] under a mix of Spanish law and British practice. [[e:sugar-plantation|Sugar]] and [[e:cacao|cacao]] estates expanded with enslaved and then free labour. From 1845 to 1917 some 143,000 Indian indentured workers arrived, bringing [[e:hinduism|Hinduism]] and [[e:islam|Islam]]. French [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] culture and [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] remained strong, and [[e:trinidad-and-tobago-carnival|Carnival]] took shape after emancipation.
colony-of-trinidad.e: In 1889 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] joined [[e:trinidad|Trinidad]] with struggling [[e:tobago|Tobago]], creating the [[s:colony-of-trinidad-and-tobago|Colony of Trinidad and Tobago]]. [[e:port-of-spain|Port of Spain]] remained the capital, and the oil industry, which began with commercial drilling in the early 20th century, soon reshaped the economy.

caranqui.t: A confederation of chiefdoms in the northern highlands of Ecuador that held out against the Incas for years before a bloody defeat at Yahuarcocha.
caranqui.o: The Caranqui, or Karanki, lived in the [[e:imbabura-province|Imbabura]] and [[e:pichincha-province|Pichincha]] highlands of northern [[s:republic-of-ecuador|Ecuador]]. From about 800 they built large earthen mounds called tolas, including platform mounds with ramps at [[e:cochasqui|Cochasquí]], and formed an alliance with neighbouring peoples such as the [[e:cayambi|Cayambi]].
caranqui.r: The Caranqui were ruled by hereditary lords who controlled farming of [[e:maize|maize]] and [[e:potato|potatoes]] on the volcanic slopes and trade with lowland peoples. Their tola mounds served as residences for chiefs, ceremonial platforms and burials. [[e:cochasqui|Cochasquí]], with fifteen pyramids, was a major centre. Local leaders were bound together by marriage and exchange rather than a single state.
caranqui.e: The [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] rulers [[e:tupac-inca-yupanqui|Túpac Inca Yupanqui]] and [[e:huayna-capac|Huayna Capac]] fought long campaigns in the north. Around 1495 Huayna Capac crushed the Caranqui and [[e:cayambi|Cayambi]] at [[e:yahuarcocha|Lake Yahuarcocha]], the 'lake of blood', named after the massacre. The region became an Inca province before the Spanish conquest.

coriosolites.t: Armorican people of northern Brittany, best known today for huge hoards of their distinctive billon coins found in Jersey.
coriosolites.o: The Coriosolites lived in the modern [[e:cotes-darmor|Côtes-d'Armor]], around the [[e:rance|Rance]] estuary. Caesar names them among the Armorican peoples who submitted to [[e:publius-licinius-crassus|Publius Crassus]] in 57 BCE.
coriosolites.r: They issued abundant coins of base [[e:silver|silver]] with stylised heads and horses. Hoards buried around the time of the Roman conquest, above all the [[e:grouville-hoard|Grouville hoard]] found in [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]] in 2012 with around 70,000 coins, suggest wealth from cross-[[e:english-channel|Channel]] trade or refugees fleeing Caesar.
coriosolites.e: After joining the [[s:veneti|Veneti]] and the [[s:unelli|Unelli]] in 56 BCE they were absorbed into [[e:gallia-lugdunensis|Gallia Lugdunensis]]. Their Roman capital was [[e:corseul|Fanum Martis]] at Corseul, with a large temple of [[e:mars-mythology|Mars]], and the name survives in Corseul.

county-of-louvain.t: The county around Leuven and Brussels from which the Reginarid counts built the Duchy of Brabant.
county-of-louvain.o: Around 1003 [[e:lambert-i-count-of-louvain|Lambert I the Bearded]], a member of the [[e:reginarids|Reginarid]] family, took the title of count of [[e:leuven|Louvain]]. He held lands around Leuven and [[e:brussels|Brussels]], which was growing on the [[e:senne|Senne]], and expanded them through war with the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Liège]] and neighbouring lords.
county-of-louvain.r: The counts ruled a fertile, densely settled region on the trade routes between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]]. [[e:brussels|Brussels]] and [[e:leuven|Leuven]] grew as market towns. [[e:godfrey-i-of-louvain|Godfrey I of Louvain]] was named duke of [[e:duchy-of-lower-lorraine|Lower Lorraine]] in 1106, giving the family the ducal title and a claim to authority over the whole region, and they also styled themselves landgraves of [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]].
county-of-louvain.e: Around 1183 Count Henry I began using the title duke of [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]], and after the [[e:diet-of-schwabisch-hall|Diet of Schwäbisch Hall]] in 1190 the county became the core of the Duchy of Brabant, whose dukes ruled from [[e:brussels|Brussels]] and [[e:leuven|Leuven]].

colony-of-niger.t: The French territory in the central Sahel and southern Sahara, ruled first as a military territory, which became independent as Niger in 1960.
colony-of-niger.o: The French conquest of the area began with the [[e:voulet-chanoine-mission|Voulet-Chanoine mission]] of 1899, notorious for massacring villagers, and the occupation of [[e:zinder|Zinder]], capital of the [[s:sultanate-of-damagaram|Sultanate of Damagaram]]. In 1900 [[e:france|France]] created a military territory, with headquarters first at Zinder. The territory became a colony of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]] in 1922, and the capital moved definitively to [[e:niamey|Niamey]] in 1926.
colony-of-niger.r: French rule was thinly spread over a vast territory of farmers in the south and [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] and [[e:toubou-people|Toubou]] herders in the [[e:sahara|Sahara]]. Tuareg resistance culminated in the revolt of [[e:kaocen-ag-mohammed|Kaocen]], who besieged [[s:sultanate-of-agadez|Agadez]] in 1916-1917. [[e:groundnut|Groundnuts]] became the main cash crop, taxes and forced labour drove migration to [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]] and [[e:ghana|Ghana]], and education reached very few.
colony-of-niger.e: After 1946 political parties emerged. [[e:djibo-bakary|Djibo Bakary's]] Sawaba party campaigned for a no vote in 1958, but [[e:hamani-diori|Hamani Diori]], backed by [[e:france|France]], prevailed. [[e:niger-river|Niger]] became an autonomous republic in December 1958 and independent on 3 August 1960, with Diori as president.

caboloan.t: The kingdom of Pangasinan on the Lingayen Gulf of Luzon, which sent envoys to Ming China and traded deerskins with Japan.
caboloan.o: The Ming records name a polity called Feng-chia-hsi-lan, identified with Pangasinan, which sent tribute missions to [[e:china|China]] in the early 15th century under a ruler named Kamayin. The people lived around the [[e:lingayen-gulf|Lingayen Gulf]] and along the [[e:agno-river|Agno River]], with their centre at [[e:san-carlos-pangasinan|Binalatongan]], later San Carlos.
caboloan.r: Caboloan was governed by a hereditary chief over a society of nobles, freemen and dependants. It exported deerskins, gold and salt, and in the 16th century Japanese traders visited, so that the Spanish called the port of [[e:agoo|Agoo]] on the gulf Puerto de Japon. Its people practised indigenous religion.
caboloan.e: Spanish forces under [[e:juan-de-salcedo|Juan de Salcedo]] reached Pangasinan in 1572, and the area was brought under Spanish rule in the following years. Pangasinan became a province of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-the-philippines|Captaincy General of the Philippines]] and its people resisted in revolts such as that of [[e:andres-malong|Andres Malong]] in 1660.

county-of-montfort.t: Lake Constance county of a branch of the counts of Tübingen, who founded Feldkirch and ruled Bregenz and Tettnang before selling out to Austria.
county-of-montfort.o: Hugo, a younger son of the Palatine Count of [[e:tubingen|Tübingen]], received lands in [[e:raetia|Rhaetia]] around 1200 and named himself after Montfort castle in [[e:vorarlberg|Vorarlberg]]. He founded the town of [[e:feldkirch|Feldkirch]]. His descendants divided into several lines, including Werdenberg, Feldkirch, [[e:bregenz|Bregenz]] and [[e:tettnang|Tettnang]], holding lands around the eastern shore of [[e:lake-constance|Lake Constance]].
county-of-montfort.r: The counts ruled castles, small towns and Alpine valleys, often allied with or dependent on the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]]. One of them, [[e:hugo-von-montfort|Hugo von Montfort]] of the [[e:bregenz|Bregenz]] line, was a noted poet of the late 14th century. Successive debts forced sales: [[e:feldkirch|Feldkirch]] passed to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1375 and Bregenz in stages in the 15th century, leaving the [[e:tettnang|Tettnang]] line as the main survivor.
county-of-montfort.e: Deeply indebted after building their palace at [[e:tettnang|Tettnang]], the counts sold the remaining county to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1779, and the line died out in 1787. Tettnang passed to [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] and then to Württemberg in 1810, while [[e:vorarlberg|Vorarlberg]] remained Austrian.

cacicazgo-of-higuey.t: The Taíno chiefdom of eastern Hispaniola, the last on the island to be conquered, ending with the execution of Cotubanamá in 1504.
cacicazgo-of-higuey.o: Higüey occupied the eastern end of [[e:hispaniola|Hispaniola]], now the eastern [[s:first-dominican-republic|Dominican Republic]]. It was one of the five principal chiefdoms when [[e:christopher-columbus|Columbus]] arrived in 1492, and its people had close contacts with [[e:puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] across the [[e:mona-passage|Mona Passage]].
cacicazgo-of-higuey.r: Higüey was ruled by paramount caciques, Cayacoa and later [[e:cotubanama|Cotubanamá]], from villages on the coastal plain. Its people were reputed fierce warriors and [[e:archery|archers]]. They farmed [[e:cassava|cassava]] and traded across the [[e:mona-passage|Mona Passage]]. Caves such as those of the present-day [[e:cotubanama-national-park|Cotubanamá National Park]] hold [[e:taino|Taíno]] rock art.
cacicazgo-of-higuey.e: Uprisings against Spanish abuses in 1503-04 were crushed by [[e:juan-de-esquivel|Juan de Esquivel]]. [[e:cotubanama|Cotubanamá]] was captured and hanged in [[e:santo-domingo|Santo Domingo]], ending the last independent chiefdom of [[e:hispaniola|Hispaniola]]. Its lands passed to the [[s:captaincy-general-of-santo-domingo|Captaincy General of Santo Domingo]].

county-of-stolberg.t: Harz county known for its mining and timber, birthplace of Thomas Müntzer, and the base of a comital family that later ruled Wernigerode.
county-of-stolberg.o: The counts of Stolberg, perhaps descended from the counts of Hohnstein, appear around 1210 with a castle above the narrow valley of Stolberg in the southern [[e:harz|Harz]]. They expanded by purchase and inheritance, gaining the County of [[e:wernigerode|Wernigerode]] in 1429 and later lands in [[e:thuringia|Thuringia]] and on the [[e:rhine|Rhine]].
county-of-stolberg.r: The county was small and hilly, its wealth drawn from [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] mining, smelting and forestry. The radical reformer [[e:thomas-muntzer|Thomas Müntzer]] was born in Stolberg around 1489. Count Botho III's daughter [[e:juliana-of-stolberg|Juliana of Stolberg]] was mother of [[e:william-the-silent|William the Silent]], and his sons introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] after his death in 1538. The counts were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of [[e:saxony|Saxony]] and of the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[e:halberstadt|Halberstadt]] for parts of their lands.
county-of-stolberg.e: In 1645 the family divided into the [[s:county-of-stolberg-wernigerode|Stolberg-Wernigerode]] and Stolberg-Stolberg lines, which later also produced Stolberg-Rossla. These remained minor rulers under [[e:saxons|Saxon]] and Prussian overlordship until mediatisation, and the old town of Stolberg survives in [[e:saxony-anhalt|Saxony-Anhalt]].

county-of-vaudemont.t: A small Lorraine county held by a cadet line of the ducal house, whose heir René II finally inherited the Duchy of Lorraine itself.
county-of-vaudemont.o: Around 1070 Duke Gerard of [[e:lorraine|Lorraine's]] younger son Gerard received the county of Vaudémont, south of [[e:nancy|Nancy]], with its castle on the hill of Sion. His descendants ruled it as a cadet branch, often at odds with the main ducal line.
county-of-vaudemont.r: Vaudémont was a modest rural county whose hill of Sion was a Marian pilgrimage site. In the 14th century it passed to the house of Joinville and then, by marriage, to Ferry of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]]. His son [[e:antoine-of-vaudemont|Antoine of Vaudémont]] claimed the Duchy of [[e:lorraine|Lorraine]] and defeated [[e:rene-of-anjou|René of Anjou]] at [[e:battle-of-bulgneville|Bulgnéville]] in 1431.
county-of-vaudemont.e: Antoine's son Ferry II married René's daughter [[e:yolande-duchess-of-lorraine|Yolande]], and their son [[e:rene-ii-duke-of-lorraine|René II]] inherited the [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Duchy of Lorraine]] in 1473, merging Vaudémont with it. The title survived as a dignity for younger members of the ducal family.

cassi.t: British people named only by Julius Caesar in 54 BCE, sometimes linked by name with Cassivellaunus, leader of resistance to Rome.
cassi.o: The Cassi are recorded once in [[e:commentarii-de-bello-gallico|Caesar's Gallic War]] as one of five British peoples, with the [[s:iceni|Cenimagni]], [[s:segontiaci|Segontiaci]], [[s:ancalites|Ancalites]] and [[s:bibroci|Bibroci]], who sent envoys to surrender during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
cassi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Because their name resembles that of [[e:cassivellaunus|Cassivellaunus]], some historians suggest they were his own people or a group within his following north of the [[e:river-thames|Thames]], perhaps in [[e:hertfordshire|Hertfordshire]], but there is no firm evidence.
cassi.e: They do not appear again in any source. Their territory, wherever it lay, was absorbed into larger polities such as the [[s:catuvellauni|Catuvellauni]] before the Roman conquest of 43.

commune-of-arezzo.t: A Ghibelline city-republic of eastern Tuscany whose defeat at Campaldino in 1289 began its long decline before the power of Florence.
commune-of-arezzo.o: [[e:arezzo|Arezzo]], an old Etruscan and Roman town, was dominated by its powerful [[e:bishop|bishops]], but consuls appear by 1098. The commune grew in the 12th century, contesting control of the town and the rural castles with the bishops and with neighbouring [[s:republic-of-siena|Siena]].
commune-of-arezzo.r: Governed by consuls, then a podestà and later priors, [[e:arezzo|Arezzo]] was generally Ghibelline. Its [[e:bishop|bishops]] remained political leaders: [[e:guglielmino-degli-ubertini|Guglielmino degli Ubertini]] died fighting [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] at [[e:battle-of-campaldino|Campaldino]] in 1289, and [[e:guido-tarlati|Guido Tarlati]], bishop from 1312 and lord of the city from 1321 until his death in 1327, expanded the city's territory and rebuilt its walls. The poet [[e:petrarch|Petrarch]] was born in the city in 1304, his family having been exiled from [[e:florence|Florence]].
commune-of-arezzo.e: After [[e:guido-tarlati|Tarlati]]'s death the city fell under outside lords and was racked by faction. In 1384 the French captain [[e:enguerrand-vii-de-coucy|Enguerrand de Coucy]] sold it to the [[s:republic-of-florence|Republic of Florence]], which ruled it for the rest of its history.

corcyra.t: Corinthian colony on Corfu that grew into a major naval power, whose clash with Corinth helped trigger the Peloponnesian War.
corcyra.o: Corinthians under [[e:chersicrates|Chersicrates]] founded Corcyra on the island of Corfu c. 733 BCE, displacing earlier Eretrian settlers. Its position on the route to [[e:italy|Italy]] and [[e:sicily|Sicily]] made it rich, and it soon broke with its mother city: [[e:thucydides|Thucydides]] dates the first Greek sea battle, between [[s:corinth|Corinth]] and Corcyra, to c. 664 BCE.
corcyra.r: Corcyra had the second-largest Greek navy by the 430s BCE. Its quarrel with [[s:corinth|Corinth]] over [[e:durres|Epidamnus]] led to battles at [[e:battle-of-leucimme|Leukimme]] and [[e:battle-of-sybota|Sybota]] and an alliance with [[s:athens|Athens]]. A brutal civil war between democrats and oligarchs from 427 BCE is described by [[e:thucydides|Thucydides]]. The temple of [[e:artemis|Artemis]] has the oldest stone Greek pediment, with a [[e:gorgon|Gorgon]].
corcyra.e: In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] Corcyra was held by [[e:agathocles-of-syracuse|Agathocles of Syracuse]] and [[e:pyrrhus-of-epirus|Pyrrhus]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-epirus|Kingdom of Epirus]]. After an Illyrian attack in 229 BCE, it placed itself under Roman protection, becoming a Roman ally and base.

celtici.t: Celtic communities of south-western Iberia, said by Pliny to have migrated from Celtiberia, living in the Alentejo and western Andalusia.
celtici.o: [[e:strabo|Strabo]] and Pliny describe Celtici in the south-west, between the [[e:guadiana|Guadiana]] and the Atlantic and in the [[e:beturia|Beturia]] region of [[e:extremadura|Extremadura]] and [[e:huelva|Huelva]]. Pliny says they came from the [[s:celtiberians|Celtiberians]], as shown by their religion, language and town names, though the date of their arrival is uncertain, probably from the 5th century BCE.
celtici.r: They lived in fortified settlements such as [[e:nertobriga-beturia|Nertobriga]] and [[e:mirobriga|Mirobriga]], whose -briga names are Celtic. Their society of farmers and herders lay close to the mining districts of the [[e:sierra-morena|Sierra Morena]]. They seem to have been a group of communities rather than a single polity.
celtici.e: Their territory was drawn into [[s:hispania-ulterior|Hispania Ulterior]] and was pacified after the Lusitanian wars and the campaigns of [[e:decimus-junius-brutus-callaicus|Decimus Junius Brutus]] from 138 BCE. Under Augustus it was split between [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]] and [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]].

colony-of-vancouver-island.t: A British colony granted to the Hudson's Bay Company in 1849 to secure the Pacific coast north of the 49th parallel, with its capital at Victoria.
colony-of-vancouver-island.o: After the [[e:oregon-treaty|Oregon Treaty]] of 1846 left [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] only the lands north of the 49th parallel, the Crown made Vancouver Island a colony in 1849 and leased it to the [[e:hudsons-bay-company|Hudson's Bay Company]] on condition that it bring settlers. Fort [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]], founded by the Company in 1843, became the capital. The first governor, [[e:richard-blanshard|Richard Blanshard]], resigned within two years.
colony-of-vancouver-island.r: [[e:james-douglas-governor|James Douglas]], the Company's chief factor, governed from 1851 to 1864. Between 1850 and 1854 he concluded fourteen land purchase agreements, the [[e:douglas-treaties|Douglas Treaties]], with [[e:lekwungen|Lekwungen]] and other [[e:first-nations-in-canada|First Nations]]. A small elected assembly, the first in western [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]], met from 1856. [[e:coal|Coal]] mines at [[e:nanaimo|Nanaimo]] and farming supplied the colony, but settlers were few until the [[e:fraser-river|Fraser River]] gold rush of 1858 turned [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]] into a boom town.
colony-of-vancouver-island.e: The Company's lease ended in 1859. Falling revenues after the gold rushes, and the costs of two separate governments, led [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to merge the island with the mainland as the [[s:colony-of-british-columbia-1858-1866|Colony of British Columbia]] in 1866.

cantiaci.t: The people of Kent, first named by Julius Caesar, whose four kings attacked his ships in 54 BCE and whose coast saw the Roman landing of 43.
cantiaci.o: Kent was the part of [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] closest to [[e:gaul|Gaul]], and [[e:julius-caesar|Caesar]] described its people as the most civilised of the [[e:britons-celtic-people|Britons]], much like the [[e:gauls|Gauls]] in custom. When he crossed in 55 and 54 BCE, Cantium was divided among four kings, [[e:cingetorix-cantium|Cingetorix]], Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax, who attacked his beached fleet at the command of [[e:cassivellaunus|Cassivellaunus]] and were driven off.
cantiaci.r: Kent was densely farmed and closely tied to the Continent, receiving Gallo-Belgic coins and producing its own issues, including early cast potin coins. Oppida grew at [[e:canterbury|Canterbury]], [[e:rochester-kent|Rochester]] and [[e:bigbury-camp|Bigbury]]. In the decades before the Claudian invasion, coins of [[e:dubnovellaunus|Dubnovellaunus]] and later the influence of [[e:cunobelinus|Cunobelinus]] of the [[s:catuvellauni|Catuvellauni]] suggest Kent fell under the sway of more powerful northern neighbours.
cantiaci.e: The Roman army landed at [[e:richborough|Richborough]] in 43, and Kent was quickly absorbed into [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]]. Its people formed the civitas of the Cantiaci, governed from [[e:canterbury|Durovernum Cantiacorum]], the later Canterbury. The old name lived on in the [[s:kingdom-of-kent|Kingdom of Kent]] and the modern county.

colony-of-aden.t: Aden as a British Crown colony, a booming port and military base whose politics fed the nationalist movement in South Arabia.
colony-of-aden.o: Under the [[e:government-of-india|Government of India]] Act of 1935, the [[s:aden-settlement|Aden Settlement]] was separated from [[s:british-raj|British India]] and became a [[e:crown-colony|Crown colony]] on 1 April 1937, governed directly from [[e:london|London]] by a governor. It covered the port of [[e:aden|Aden]], Crater, Steamer Point and [[e:little-aden|Little Aden]].
colony-of-aden.r: [[e:aden|Aden]] was one of the world's busiest ports, serving ships on the Suez route. A [[e:bp|British Petroleum]] refinery opened at [[e:little-aden|Little Aden]] in 1954, and from 1960 Aden housed [[e:britain|Britain's]] [[e:middle-east|Middle East]] Command. The population of Yemenis, Indians, [[e:somalis|Somalis]] and a dwindling Jewish community grew rapidly, and strong trade unions, led by the [[e:aden-trades-union-congress|Aden Trades Union Congress]], became the base of anti-colonial politics.
colony-of-aden.e: In January 1963, against nationalist opposition, the colony joined the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] and became the [[s:state-of-aden|State of Aden]].
colony-of-aden.re: Islam, with Hindu, Jewish and Christian minorities

canton-of-valencia.t: A federalist canton proclaimed in Valencia during the Cantonal Rebellion of 1873 and suppressed within weeks.
canton-of-valencia.o: In July 1873 radical federalists in [[e:valencia|Valencia]], frustrated by the [[s:spanish-first-republic|Spanish First Republic]]'s failure to build a federal state, formed a revolutionary junta and proclaimed the city a sovereign canton, joining the rising begun in the [[s:canton-of-cartagena|Canton of Cartagena]].
canton-of-valencia.r: The junta took over city government and local forces and declared its intention to belong to a federal [[e:spain|Spain]] built by free cantons. Like the other cantons, it had little time to put any programme into practice.
canton-of-valencia.e: Government troops under General [[e:arsenio-martinez-campos|Arsenio Martínez Campos]] besieged and bombarded the city, and the canton surrendered in early August 1873.

county-of-stolberg-wernigerode.t: Harz county of the Stolberg family, a centre of German Pietism dominated from its castle above Wernigerode.
county-of-stolberg-wernigerode.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-stolberg|Stolberg]] acquired [[e:wernigerode|Wernigerode]] in 1429. Repeated divisions of the family lands produced a separate line of Stolberg-Wernigerode in 1645, ruling the town and the northern [[e:harz|Harz]] around the [[e:brocken|Brocken]].
county-of-stolberg-wernigerode.r: The county had [[e:silver|silver]] and iron mining and forestry in the [[e:harz|Harz]]. In 1714 a treaty acknowledged the overlordship of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], limiting the counts' independence. Under [[e:christian-ernst-count-of-stolberg-wernigerode|Christian Ernst]], from 1710 to 1771, the court became a centre of [[e:pietism|Pietism]], with hymn books, a fine library and links to [[e:halle-saale|Halle]], and the counts supported church and school reforms.
county-of-stolberg-wernigerode.e: The county was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] in 1807 and passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815, while the family kept its estates. Its counts were later raised to princes, and [[e:otto-prince-of-stolberg-wernigerode|Otto of Stolberg-Wernigerode]] served as Prussian vice-chancellor under Bismarck.

ciarraige-luachra.t: North Kerry kingdom of the Ciarraige, the people who gave County Kerry its name, later ruled by the O'Connor Kerry family.
ciarraige-luachra.o: The Ciarraige, 'people of Ciar', were one of several groups of that name in early Ireland, claiming descent from a legendary ancestor Ciar. The Ciarraige Luachra held north Kerry around [[e:tralee|Tralee]] and the [[e:river-feale|Feale]] valley from the early [[e:middle-ages|medieval period]], as a subject people paying tribute to the [[e:eoganachta|Eóganachta]] kings of the [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Kingdom of Munster]].
ciarraige-luachra.r: Their kingdom was a land of bog, upland and coastal plain, and its wealth lay in [[e:cattle|cattle]]. St [[e:brendan-the-navigator|Brendan the Navigator]], founder of [[e:clonfert|Clonfert]], was traditionally born in their territory near [[e:tralee|Tralee]], and the region had a lively church life. Their kings, from the 11th century known as [[e:oconnor-kerry|Ó Conchobhair Chiarraí]], O'Connor Kerry, held a respected place among the lesser kings of [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]].
ciarraige-luachra.e: In the 13th century [[e:anglo-normans|Anglo-Norman]] lords, especially the [[e:fitzgerald-dynasty|FitzGeralds]], took much of their land, and the [[e:oconnor-kerry|O'Connors Kerry]] were confined to the north of the county, in [[e:iraghticonnor|Iraghticonnor]], ruled from [[e:carrigafoyle-castle|Carrigafoyle Castle]] until the late 16th century. The people's name lives on in [[e:county-kerry|County Kerry]].

ceibal.t: A Maya city on the Pasión river with one of the oldest ceremonial plazas in the lowlands, which unusually flourished during the Terminal Classic collapse.
ceibal.o: Ceibal (Seibal) was founded about 1000 BCE, when early villagers built a ceremonial plaza, making it among the earliest Maya centres. After a Preclassic peak and a period of decline, a royal dynasty is recorded in the Classic period from around 400 CE.
ceibal.r: In 735 Ceibal was conquered by [[s:dos-pilas|Dos Pilas]], whose king captured its ruler [[e:yichaak-bahlam|Yich'aak B'ahlam]], and it became a subordinate centre. After the fall of the [[e:petexbatun|Petexbatun]] kingdom, Ceibal revived under the lord [[e:watul-katel|Wat'ul K'atel]], installed in 829, whose stelae show foreign-looking dress and new styles, perhaps linked to [[e:gulf-coast-of-mexico|Gulf Coast]] or northern contacts.
ceibal.e: Ceibal was one of the last southern lowland cities to raise monuments, until about 889, and was abandoned by about 930. Its long sequence makes it important for studying both the origins and the collapse of Maya civilisation.

colony-of-saint-christopher.t: England's first colony in the Caribbean, founded on Saint Kitts in 1623, which served as the 'mother colony' of the English West Indies.
colony-of-saint-christopher.o: [[e:thomas-warner|Thomas Warner]] landed on [[e:saint-kitts|Saint Christopher]] (Saint Kitts) with a small group of settlers in 1623, founding the first English colony in the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]]. Arriving French settlers shared the island, and in 1626 the two groups massacred the [[e:kalinago|Kalinago]] inhabitants at Bloody Point.
colony-of-saint-christopher.r: From 1627 the island was partitioned, with the English holding the centre and the French the ends. English settlers spread from there to [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]], [[s:colony-of-antigua|Antigua]] and [[s:montserrat|Montserrat]]. Tobacco gave way to [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], worked by enslaved Africans. The English and French fought repeatedly over the island, and from 1671 it belonged to the [[s:leeward-islands-colony|Leeward Islands colony]].
colony-of-saint-christopher.e: The [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 gave [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] the whole island. The French captured [[e:brimstone-hill-fortress|Brimstone Hill]] in 1782 but returned it in 1783. In 1882 [[e:saint-kitts|Saint Christopher]] was joined with [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]] and [[e:anguilla|Anguilla]] as [[s:saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla|Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla]].

commune-of-san-gimignano.t: A small Tuscan hill-town republic on the pilgrim road to Rome, whose surviving medieval towers make it the best-preserved image of a communal city.
commune-of-san-gimignano.o: San Gimignano grew on the [[e:via-francigena|Via Francigena]], the pilgrim route from northern [[e:europe|Europe]] to [[e:rome|Rome]], and won self-government from the [[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:commune-of-volterra|Volterra]]; by 1199 it was an independent commune under consuls.
commune-of-san-gimignano.r: The town prospered from pilgrims, trade and especially saffron, grown in the surrounding hills and sold as far as [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. Rival families, led by the Ardinghelli and the Salvucci, built tower houses as symbols of wealth and power; around 72 are said to have stood, and 14 survive. [[e:dante-alighieri|Dante]] came as an envoy of [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] in 1300. The [[e:collegiata-san-gimignano|Collegiata]] church was frescoed by Sienese painters.
commune-of-san-gimignano.e: The [[e:black-death|Black Death]] of 1348 and the decline of the pilgrim trade left the town poor and exhausted by feuds. In 1353 it submitted to the [[s:republic-of-florence|Republic of Florence]], and its towers survived because it stopped growing.

chiefdom-of-hawaii-island.t: The chiefdom of Hawaiʻi Island, largest of the Hawaiian islands, from which Kamehameha I launched the conquests that created the Kingdom of Hawaii.
chiefdom-of-hawaii-island.o: Around 1500 [[e:umi-a-liloa|ʻUmi-a-Līloa]], son of the ruler [[e:liloa|Līloa]], overthrew his half-brother [[e:hakau|Hākau]] and united the island's six districts under one aliʻi nui. Tradition credits him with reorganising land into ahupuaʻa, wedge-shaped units running from mountain to sea, and building stone temples. His successors ruled from royal centres such as [[e:waipio-valley|Waipiʻo Valley]] and [[e:kailua-kona|Kailua-Kona]].
chiefdom-of-hawaii-island.r: The aliʻi nui stood at the head of a hierarchy of chiefs, priests and land managers enforced by the kapu system, and the island's dryland field systems in [[e:kona-hawaii|Kona]] and [[e:kohala-hawaii|Kohala]] fed a large population. Rival lines fought for the title. The ruler [[e:kalaniopuu|Kalaniʻōpuʻu]] received [[e:james-cook|James Cook]] at [[e:kealakekua-bay|Kealakekua Bay]] in 1779, and Cook was killed there in a clash that February.
chiefdom-of-hawaii-island.e: After [[e:kalaniopuu|Kalaniʻōpuʻu]] died in 1782, his nephew [[e:kamehameha-i|Kamehameha]] defeated [[e:kiwalao|Kiwalaʻō]] at [[e:battle-of-mokuohai|Mokuʻōhai]] and, after years of war, won the whole island by 1791. Conquering the [[s:chiefdom-of-maui|Chiefdom of Maui]] and the [[s:chiefdom-of-oahu|Chiefdom of Oahu]], he founded the [[s:kingdom-of-hawaii|Kingdom of Hawaii]] in 1795.

commune-of-modena.t: An Emilian city-republic whose Romanesque cathedral is a masterpiece of medieval sculpture, and Bologna's lasting rival on the Via Emilia.
commune-of-modena.o: [[e:modena|Modena]] had belonged to the lands of [[e:matilda-of-tuscany|Matilda of Canossa]], and its cathedral was begun in 1099 by the architect [[e:lanfranco-architect|Lanfranco]] with sculpture by [[e:wiligelmo|Wiligelmo]]. After Matilda's death the citizens organised a commune, with consuls recorded by 1135.
commune-of-modena.r: The commune was governed by consuls, later a podestà and popular councils. [[e:modena|Modena]] was usually Ghibelline and fought a long rivalry with [[e:guelphs-and-ghibellines|Guelph]] [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] over borders and water rights in the plain. Its cathedral and the [[e:ghirlandina|Ghirlandina]] bell tower became symbols of civic identity. Factional wars between noble families, the Grasolfi and Aigoni, crippled the government in the later 13th century.
commune-of-modena.e: In 1288 the city gave lordship to [[e:obizzo-ii-deste|Obizzo II d'Este]] of the [[s:duchy-of-ferrara|Duchy of Ferrara]]. Apart from brief interruptions, the [[e:house-of-este|Este]] held [[e:modena|Modena]] from then on, and it later became the capital of the [[s:duchy-of-modena-and-reggio|Duchy of Modena and Reggio]].

chamba-state.t: A Himalayan hill kingdom in the Ravi valley ruled by one dynasty for some 1,400 years, known for its stone temples, copper-plate grants and Chamba rumal embroidery.
chamba-state.o: Tradition holds that the state was founded around 550 by Maru, a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] of the Varman line, with its first capital at [[e:bharmour|Brahmapura]] (modern Bharmour) in the upper [[e:ravi|Ravi]] valley. In the 10th century Raja [[e:sahil-varman|Sahil Varman]] moved the capital down the valley to Chamba, named, by tradition, after his daughter Champavati.
chamba-state.r: Chamba is unusually well documented for a hill state, thanks to many [[e:copper|copper]]-plate land grants and inscriptions. Its Rajas built the [[e:lakshmi-narayan-temple-chamba|Lakshmi Narayan]] temple complex and patronised Pahari [[e:persian-miniature|miniature painting]] and the embroidered Chamba rumal. Remote and mountainous, it accepted Mughal overlordship, paid tribute to the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] and kept most internal affairs in its own hands.
chamba-state.e: After the [[e:first-anglo-sikh-war|First Anglo-Sikh War]] in 1846 the British confirmed the Rajas in their state. Raja [[e:bhuri-singh|Bhuri Singh]] (1904–1919) founded the museum that bears his name. Chamba merged into the new province of [[e:himachal-pradesh|Himachal Pradesh]] in April 1948 and is now a district of [[e:india|India]].

captaincy-general-of-cuba.t: Spain's largest Caribbean colony, whose port of Havana anchored the treasure fleets and whose sugar economy became the richest in the world.
captaincy-general-of-cuba.o: [[e:diego-velazquez-de-cuellar|Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar]] led the conquest of [[e:cuba|Cuba]] from 1511, founding [[e:baracoa|Baracoa]] and other towns; the [[e:taino|Taíno]] chief [[e:hatuey|Hatuey]], who resisted, was burnt in 1512. [[e:havana|Havana]], moved to its present site around 1519, became the island's main city and, from 1607, its capital.
captaincy-general-of-cuba.r: [[e:havana|Havana]] was the gathering port of the treasure fleets returning to [[e:spain|Spain]] and was heavily fortified. The British occupied it in 1762-63. After the [[e:haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]] of the 1790s [[e:cuba|Cuba]] became the world's leading [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] producer, relying on hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans; [[e:slavery|slavery]] lasted until 1886. Captains-general such as [[e:miguel-tacon|Miguel Tacón]] ruled with broad powers.
captaincy-general-of-cuba.e: The [[e:ten-years-war|Ten Years' War]] of 1868-78, led by the [[s:republic-of-cuba-in-arms|Republic of Cuba in Arms]], and the war of 1895 challenged Spanish rule. After [[s:united-states|United States]] intervention in 1898, [[e:spain|Spain]] gave up the island, which passed to the [[s:united-states-military-government-in-cuba|United States Military Government in Cuba]].
