chikulamayembe-state.t: A Tumbuka kingdom of northern Malawi founded by ivory traders from east of Lake Malawi, destroyed by Ngoni invaders in the 1850s.
chikulamayembe-state.o: [[e:tumbuka-people|Tumbuka]] tradition recalls that in the late 18th century traders known as the [[e:balowoka|Balowoka]] crossed [[e:lake-malawi|Lake Malawi]] from the east seeking [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]]. Their leader settled near Bolero and gained authority over local Tumbuka clans, founding the Chikulamayembe dynasty.
chikulamayembe-state.r: The Chikulamayembe built power on control of the [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] trade towards the lake and the coast, distributing imported cloth and [[e:bead|beads]] to secure the loyalty of clan heads. Authority over the scattered [[e:tumbuka-people|Tumbuka]] population remained loose, and the state relied on trade rather than a strong military.
chikulamayembe-state.e: In the 1850s the [[e:ngoni|Ngoni]] under the successors of [[e:zwangendaba|Zwangendaba]] invaded northern [[e:malawi|Malawi]] and destroyed the kingdom, incorporating many [[e:tumbuka-people|Tumbuka]]. The British later restored the Chikulamayembe title as a chieftaincy in 1907.

cavares.t: Gallic people of the lower Rhône whose towns became Avignon, Cavaillon and Orange.
cavares.o: [[e:strabo|Strabo]] names the Cavares as the leading people between the [[e:durance|Durance]] and the [[e:isere-river|Isère]], east of the [[e:rhone|Rhône]]. Their towns included [[e:avignon|Avennio]] (Avignon), [[e:cavaillon|Cabellio]] (Cavaillon) and [[e:orange-vaucluse|Arausio]] ([[s:principality-of-orange|Orange]]), and they had close commercial ties with [[s:massalia|Massalia]].
cavares.r: [[e:strabo|Strabo]] describes them as already largely Romanised in his day. Little is known of their earlier rulers.
cavares.e: They came under [[e:rome|Rome]] after 121 BCE. In 105 BCE the [[e:cimbri|Cimbri]] and [[e:teutones|Teutones]] destroyed two Roman armies at [[e:orange-vaucluse|Arausio]] in their land, one of Rome's worst defeats. Arausio was refounded as a colony for veterans of the Second [[e:legion|Legion]], with its famous [[e:theatre|theatre]] and arch.

commandancy-general-of-the-internal-prov.t: Military command created by Bourbon Spain to defend the vast northern frontier of New Spain, from Texas and New Mexico to Sonora and the Californias.
commandancy-general-of-the-internal-prov.o: Under the reforms of [[e:jose-de-galvez|José de Gálvez]], [[e:charles-iii-of-spain|Charles III]] separated the northern provinces of [[s:new-spain|New Spain]] from the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]]'s direct control in 1776 to strengthen frontier defence against the [[e:apache|Apache]] and [[e:comanche|Comanche]]. [[e:teodoro-de-croix|Teodoro de Croix]] became the first commandant general, with his seat at [[e:arizpe|Arizpe]] in [[e:sonora|Sonora]], later moved to [[e:chihuahua-city|Chihuahua]].
commandancy-general-of-the-internal-prov.r: The commandant general held military, political and judicial authority over [[s:nueva-vizcaya|Nueva Vizcaya]], [[e:sonora|Sonora]] and [[e:sinaloa|Sinaloa]], the [[e:the-californias|Californias]], [[e:santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico|New Mexico]], [[e:coahuila|Coahuila]] and [[e:texas|Texas]], and at times [[e:nuevo-leon|Nuevo León]] and [[s:nuevo-santander|Nuevo Santander]]. The command rested on a chain of presidios, mounted soldiers and alliances or peace treaties with indigenous groups, notably the 1786 [[e:comanche|Comanche]] peace in [[e:new-mexico|New Mexico]]. It was repeatedly reorganised, divided into eastern and western commands and placed back under the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]].
commandancy-general-of-the-internal-prov.e: The command continued, in eastern and western halves after 1813, until Mexican independence in 1821. Its territories became states and territories of [[s:mexico|Mexico]], and much of its north, including [[e:texas|Texas]], [[e:santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico|New Mexico]] and [[e:california|California]], passed to the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1848.

canton-of-fribourg.t: A bilingual city-state founded by the Zähringen dukes on the Saane, which shook off Savoy in 1477 and joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1481.
canton-of-fribourg.o: Duke [[e:berthold-iv-of-zahringen|Berthold IV of Zähringen]] founded Fribourg in 1157 on a rocky bend of the [[e:sarine|Saane]]. It passed to the [[e:house-of-kyburg|Kyburgs]] and the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] and in 1452 to the [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Duchy of Savoy]]. After fighting beside the Swiss in the [[e:burgundian-wars|Burgundian Wars]], it was released by Savoy and became a free imperial city in 1478, joining the [[s:confederate-states-of-america|Confederacy]] in 1481 together with [[s:canton-of-solothurn|Solothurn]].
canton-of-fribourg.r: A small circle of patrician families ruled the city and its rural territory, which straddled the language border between French and German. Fribourg prospered from cloth and leather in the 15th century. It remained Catholic during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and became a centre of the [[e:counter-reformation|Counter-Reformation]]: Saint [[e:peter-canisius|Peter Canisius]] founded the [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] college of Saint Michael there in 1582.
canton-of-fribourg.e: The patrician regime fell to the French invasion of 1798, and Fribourg became part of the [[s:helvetic-republic|Helvetic Republic]]. Restored as a canton in 1803, it remains a bilingual Swiss canton.

caleti.t: Belgic people of the chalk coast of upper Normandy who gave their name to the Pays de Caux.
caleti.o: The Caleti lived on the plateau between the lower [[e:seine|Seine]] and the [[e:english-channel|Channel]] cliffs. Caesar reports that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
caleti.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Their coast and the [[e:seine|Seine]] estuary gave them a part in cross-[[e:english-channel|Channel]] trade.
caleti.e: They submitted in 57 BCE but sent men to [[e:battle-of-alesia|Alesia]] in 52 BCE and joined the [[s:bellovaci|Bellovaci]] in 51 BCE. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their chief town was [[e:lillebonne|Juliobona]] (Lillebonne), whose [[e:theatre|theatre]] survives, and the region kept their name as the [[e:pays-de-caux|Pays de Caux]].

corieltauvi.t: East Midlands people who issued coins under paired rulers and buried the Hallaton Treasure, and who passed under Roman rule largely without resistance.
corieltauvi.o: The Corieltauvi occupied [[e:leicestershire|Leicestershire]], [[e:lincolnshire|Lincolnshire]], [[e:nottinghamshire|Nottinghamshire]] and parts of the surrounding counties in the late [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]]; the older name Coritani was corrected after an inscription naming them was found. They grew from local farming communities on the river valleys and wolds, with major centres at [[e:leicester|Leicester]], Old Sleaford and [[e:lincoln-england|Lincoln]].
corieltauvi.r: From the late 1st century BCE they issued gold and [[e:silver|silver]] coins, often with two names together, such as VEP CORF or AVN COST, which may point to joint rule; later issues name Volisios and Dumnocoveros. The [[e:hallaton-treasure|Hallaton Treasure]], a ritual hoard of more than 5,000 coins and a Roman cavalry helmet, shows close contact with [[e:rome|Rome]] before the conquest. Pottery and [[e:iron-working|iron-working]] flourished.
corieltauvi.e: The region was occupied soon after 43, apparently with little fighting, and by the late 40s Roman forts held the area; the legio IX was later based at [[e:lincoln-england|Lincoln]]. The people formed the civitas of the Corieltauvi, governed from [[e:ratae-corieltauvorum|Ratae Corieltauvorum]], modern [[e:leicester|Leicester]], within [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]].

caracol.t: A major Classic Maya kingdom in the Maya Mountains of Belize, which defeated Tikal in 562 and grew into a sprawling garden city linked by causeways.
caracol.o: Caracol, anciently Oxwitza', was settled by about 600 BCE on a plateau in western [[s:belize|Belize]]. Its royal dynasty is counted from [[e:te-kab-chaak|Te' K'ab Chaak]], who took the throne in 331 CE, and the city grew steadily through the [[e:early-classic-period|Early Classic]].
caracol.r: Allied with the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]], Caracol under [[e:yajaw-te-kinich-ii|Yajaw Te' K'inich II]] defeated [[s:tikal|Tikal]] in 562, and [[e:kan-ii|K'an II]] later fought [[s:naranjo|Naranjo]], recording his victories on monuments including a hieroglyphic stairway found at Naranjo. The city spread over some 200 square kilometres of agricultural terraces and [[e:reservoir|reservoirs]], with causeways radiating from the centre and a population that may have exceeded 100,000.
caracol.e: Building continued later than at many lowland cities, with a last dated monument in 859, but Caracol was abandoned by about 900 CE. Excavations since 1985 have made it a key case for understanding Maya urbanism.

county-of-pallars-jussa.t: The lower half of the Pyrenean county of Pallars, centred on Tremp, which passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1192.
county-of-pallars-jussa.o: When Count Sunyer of [[e:pallars|Pallars]] died in 1011, his lands were divided between his sons: [[e:ramon-iii-of-pallars-jussa|Ramon III]] received the southern, lower part around [[e:tremp|Tremp]] and the [[e:noguera-pallaresa|Noguera Pallaresa]] valley, while his brother [[e:guillem-ii-of-pallars-sobira|Guillem]] took the mountainous north, the [[s:county-of-pallars-sobira|County of Pallars Sobirà]].
county-of-pallars-jussa.r: [[e:pallars|Pallars]] Jussà was a frontier county facing the [[s:taifa-of-lerida|Taifa of Lérida]] and expanded south by conquest. Its counts were often at odds with their cousins in the north and with the powerful frontier lord [[e:arnau-mir-de-tost|Arnau Mir de Tost]]. Like other Catalan counties, it was organised through castles, feudal oaths and religious foundations such as the canonry of [[e:santa-maria-de-mur|Santa Maria de Mur]], established by the counts in 1069.
county-of-pallars-jussa.e: In 1192 Countess Dolça bequeathed the county to [[e:alfonso-ii-of-aragon|Alfonso II of Aragon]], who incorporated it into the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]]. Its lands later formed part of the [[s:principality-of-catalonia|Principality of Catalonia]].

captaincy-of-espirito-santo.t: A Portuguese captaincy on Brazil's southeastern coast founded in 1535, which survived indigenous wars and pirate raids to become a province and state of Brazil.
captaincy-of-espirito-santo.o: In 1534 [[e:john-iii-of-portugal|King John III]] granted the captaincy of Espírito Santo to [[e:vasco-fernandes-coutinho|Vasco Fernandes Coutinho]], who landed in 1535 and founded [[e:vila-velha|Vila Velha]]. Attacks by the [[e:goitaca|Goitacá]] and other peoples forced settlers to move to an island, where the town of [[e:vitoria-espirito-santo|Vitória]] was founded in 1551 and became the capital.
captaincy-of-espirito-santo.r: Espírito Santo grew [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and was a base for [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions, including that of [[e:jose-de-anchieta|José de Anchieta]], who died there in 1597. The captaincy remained small and poor, raided by French, English and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] privateers. In the 18th century the crown discouraged roads into the interior to protect the gold district of [[s:captaincy-of-minas-gerais|Minas Gerais]].
captaincy-of-espirito-santo.e: The crown bought the captaincy from its proprietors in 1718, and it was placed under [[e:bahia|Bahia]] before regaining its own governor in 1810. In 1821 it became a province, and later a state of the Republic of [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]].

carnatic-sultanate.t: The state of the Nawabs of Arcot in south-east India, whose succession wars drew Britain and France into their struggle for India.
carnatic-sultanate.o: The [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] conquered the Carnatic region after the fall of the [[s:golconda-sultanate|Golconda Sultanate]] and the [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]]. In 1692 [[e:aurangzeb|Aurangzeb]] appointed [[e:zulfiqar-khan|Zulfiqar Ali Khan]] as Nawab of the Carnatic, and the governorship, based at [[e:arcot|Arcot]], became hereditary under [[e:saadatullah-khan-i|Saadatullah Khan]], nominally subordinate to the [[e:nizam-of-hyderabad|Nizam of Hyderabad]].
carnatic-sultanate.r: The Nawabs ruled a largely [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] Tamil and [[e:telugu-language|Telugu]] population through local chiefs and revenue farmers. [[e:chanda-sahib|Chanda Sahib]] seized [[e:madurai|Madurai]] in 1736. Rival claims between Chanda Sahib, backed by the French, and [[e:muhammad-ali-khan-wallajah|Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah]], backed by the British, led to the [[e:carnatic-wars|Carnatic Wars]] and the siege of [[e:arcot|Arcot]] in 1751, a turning point in British fortunes.
carnatic-sultanate.e: [[e:muhammad-ali-khan-wallajah|Muhammad Ali Wallajah]] won but fell deep into debt to British creditors. In 1801 the [[e:east-india-company|British East India Company]] took over the administration, leaving the nawabs a titular role, and in 1855 the title was abolished under the doctrine of lapse. [[e:the-prince|The Prince]] of [[e:arcot|Arcot]] title survives.

cyzicus.t: Milesian colony on the Sea of Marmara whose electrum coins circulated across the Greek world and which withstood Mithridates in 73 BCE.
cyzicus.o: Cyzicus was founded by [[s:miletus|Miletus]] on the isthmus of the [[e:kapidag-peninsula|Arctonnesus]] peninsula, on the southern shore of the [[e:sea-of-marmara|Propontis]]; the register follows the date c. 675 BCE, while an earlier foundation c. 756 BCE is also recorded. Its two harbours made it a natural stopping point on the route to the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]].
cyzicus.r: From the 6th century BCE Cyzicus issued electrum staters, the '[[e:cyzicene|Cyzicenes]]', widely used in trade. It was ruled by the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] and paid tribute in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. In 410 BCE [[e:alcibiades|Alcibiades]] destroyed a Spartan fleet off the city. In the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] Cyzicus was a close ally of the [[s:kingdom-of-pergamon|Kingdom of Pergamon]].
cyzicus.e: Cyzicus withstood a long siege by [[e:mithridates-vi-of-pontus|Mithridates]] in 73 BCE until [[e:lucius-licinius-lucullus|Lucullus]] relieved it, and [[e:rome|Rome]] rewarded it as a free city. It lost that status in 20 BCE, regained it, and lost it finally under [[e:tiberius|Tiberius]] in 25 CE.

captaincy-of-ilheus.t: A hereditary Portuguese captaincy on the coast of southern Bahia, troubled by indigenous wars, which much later became the heart of Brazil's cacao country.
captaincy-of-ilheus.o: In 1534 [[e:john-iii-of-portugal|King John III]] granted the Captaincy of [[e:ilheus|Ilhéus]], south of the [[e:bay-of-all-saints|Bay of All Saints]], to [[e:jorge-de-figueiredo-correia|Jorge de Figueiredo Correia]], a royal official who never went there. His lieutenant Francisco Romero founded the town of São Jorge dos Ilhéus around 1536.
captaincy-of-ilheus.r: The captaincy developed [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] mills along the rivers, and for a time it was one of the more promising settlements. From the mid-16th century repeated attacks by the [[e:aimore|Aimoré]] people destroyed mills and drove settlers away, and the population remained small. [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] missions were founded among indigenous groups. The captaincy passed through several proprietors, including the merchant Lucas Giraldes.
captaincy-of-ilheus.e: As part of [[e:marquis-of-pombal|Pombal]]'s reforms abolishing private captaincies, the crown took over [[e:ilheus|Ilhéus]] in 1761, and it was later attached to [[e:bahia|Bahia]]. In the 19th century the region became [[e:brazil|Brazil's]] main [[e:cacao|cacao]]-growing area, celebrated in the novels of [[e:jorge-amado|Jorge Amado]].

chavin.t: A highland religious centre in Peru whose temple, feline-serpent art and cult spread across much of the central Andes, forming one of the first shared cultural horizons of South America.
chavin.o: Chavín de Huántar, at the meeting of the Mosna and Huachecsa rivers in the [[e:ancash-region|Ancash]] highlands, was built from around 900 BCE as a temple complex on a route between the coast and the [[e:amazon|Amazon]] basin. Its Old Temple, a U-shaped stone platform honeycombed with galleries, grew over centuries into a larger New Temple.
chavin.r: Chavín appears to have been a centre of pilgrimage and oracle rather than a conquering state, run by a priestly elite. Inside the Old Temple stands the [[e:lanzon|Lanzón]], a carved granite monolith of a fanged deity. Priests used [[e:san-pedro-cactus|San Pedro cactus]] and other hallucinogens, and the galleries were designed to channel water and sound. Its art of jaguars, caymans, eagles and snakes appears on textiles, pottery and goldwork far beyond the site, suggesting a widely shared cult.
chavin.e: The influence of Chavín faded between about 500 and 200 BCE as regional cultures such as [[s:paracas|Paracas]] and later [[s:moche|Moche]] and [[s:nazca|Nazca]] developed their own styles. The site was damaged by later occupation and landslides. It was inscribed as a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1985.
